# Foundational NeRF: A Continuous 5D Radiance Field Learned Through Differentiable Volume Rendering

## Abstract

Foundational NeRF solves per-scene novel-view synthesis by fitting a continuous, scene-specific MLP to posed 2D images. The field maps a 3D position and viewing direction to RGB color and scalar density, with density constrained to depend only on position while color may vary with view direction. For each camera ray, the network is queried at sampled points; density and interval length form alpha values, transmittance accounts for earlier occlusion, and differentiable alpha compositing produces ray color. Photometric loss can therefore update color and density without 3D labels. Positional encoding and hierarchical coarse-to-fine sampling support high-frequency detail and allocate queries toward visually important ray regions. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:abstract:claim:c90f7f8b0c04] [E:arxiv:2306.03000:section:unknown:1:880006b63539:claim:d78338514d87] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:3_neural_radiance_field_scene_representation:0:e6a7774107f3:claim:2f4a62451a0d] [E:arxiv:2306.03000:section:unknown:2:26aa95755737:claim:d216ece2b6d6] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:3_neural_radiance_field_scene_representation:0:e6a7774107f3:claim:635a242c0596] [E:arxiv:2408.03356:section:abstract:4:1447cd6be2ee:claim:6dac674e7eed] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:5_2_hierarchical_volume_sampling:0:7c4cd481bcd3:claim:c7a0415d23ab] [E:arxiv:2211.15977:abstract:claim:c6d4c4258c8e]

## Introduction

This review is organized around the foundational NeRF pipeline rather than later acceleration or application-specific variants: first define the continuous scene representation, then explain how camera rays are sampled and volume-rendered into pixels, and finally identify the optimization and applicability boundaries that motivate later work. The user's question is therefore scoped to the original neural radiance field representation and its differentiable rendering formulation, not to real-time baking, mesh extraction, editing, generative priors, or task-specific NeRF extensions. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:abstract:claim:c90f7f8b0c04] [E:arxiv:2306.03000:abstract:claim:342e1123f513]

NeRF addresses novel view synthesis from a sparse set of posed images. Instead of explicitly reconstructing a discrete mesh or voxelized object, the original method represents a scene as a continuous volumetric function: a fully connected, non-convolutional network takes a single 5D coordinate consisting of a 3D spatial location and a 2D viewing direction, and returns the volume density and view-dependent emitted radiance at that location. Views are synthesized by querying this function along camera rays and projecting the queried colors and densities into an image with classical volume rendering. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:abstract:claim:c90f7f8b0c04] [E:arxiv:2306.03000:section:unknown:1:880006b63539:claim:d78338514d87]

In the concrete architecture, the viewing direction is represented in practice by a 3D Cartesian unit vector, so the network maps position and direction to an RGB color and scalar density. A key structural constraint separates geometry from appearance: density is predicted from position alone, while color may depend on both position and viewing direction. The original MLP first processes the 3D coordinate through eight fully connected ReLU layers with 256 channels, outputs density and a 256-dimensional feature vector, concatenates that feature with the ray direction, and uses an additional ReLU layer with 128 channels to produce the view-dependent RGB color. This factorization encourages multiview-consistent occupancy while allowing non-Lambertian appearance such as specular variation. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:3_neural_radiance_field_scene_representation:0:e6a7774107f3:claim:2f4a62451a0d] [E:arxiv:2306.03000:section:unknown:2:26aa95755737:claim:d216ece2b6d6]

The rendering operator is the bridge between the continuous field and supervised 2D images. For each pixel, NeRF casts a camera ray, evaluates 5D coordinates at sampled points along it, composites the resulting colors and densities with differentiable volume rendering, and compares the rendered pixel color with the observed image. Because this compositing procedure is differentiable, gradients from the image reconstruction loss update the MLP weights using only training images and their known camera poses. The original method also uses positional encoding to expose high-frequency coordinate variation and hierarchical coarse-to-fine sampling to concentrate evaluations where they are expected to affect the rendered ray; these are components of the foundational training strategy, distinct from later systems that replace or cache the MLP for speed. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:3_neural_radiance_field_scene_representation:0:e6a7774107f3:claim:2f4a62451a0d] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:5_2_hierarchical_volume_sampling:0:7c4cd481bcd3:claim:c7a0415d23ab] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:abstract:claim:c90f7f8b0c04]

## Background and Method Taxonomy

For this review, the organizing choice is a pipeline-based grouping of NeRF concepts: scene representation, ray evaluation and volume integration, optimization from posed images, and later system objectives that alter the representation or renderer. This grouping is used only to explain the foundational method and its boundaries; it is not a universal taxonomy and should not be attributed to the original NeRF paper as a formal classification of the field. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:abstract:claim:c90f7f8b0c04] [E:arxiv:2306.03000:abstract:claim:342e1123f513]

The first classification criterion is what a method stores or queries. The foundational NeRF is a continuous, scene-specific neural field represented by an MLP: a 3D position and viewing direction are network inputs, while density and emitted color are outputs. This differs from explicitly cached or decomposed scene structures such as sparse tensors, low-rank tensors, hash tables, and their combinations, which later work uses to change training, rendering, memory, or editing trade-offs rather than to define the original 5D radiance-field formulation. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:abstract:claim:c90f7f8b0c04] [E:arxiv:2211.15977:abstract:claim:c6d4c4258c8e] [E:arxiv:2211.15977:section:abstract:1:c074867b981e:claim:0686c20a07f2]

A second criterion is the dependence pattern of the outputs. In foundational NeRF, density is constrained to be a function of position alone, whereas RGB color is allowed to depend on both position and viewing direction. That distinction separates the view-invariant occupancy field used for compositing geometry from the view-dependent radiance term used to express appearance changes such as specularities; it is not the same as explicitly decomposing materials, lighting, normals, or reflections. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:3_neural_radiance_field_scene_representation:0:e6a7774107f3:claim:2f4a62451a0d] [E:arxiv:2306.03000:section:unknown:2:26aa95755737:claim:d216ece2b6d6]

A third criterion is how samples become pixels. The foundational renderer casts a ray for each pixel, evaluates the field at multiple positions along that ray, converts density and segment length into opacity, accumulates color with transmittance, and differentiates the resulting composite against observed images. Hierarchical coarse-to-fine sampling is an allocation strategy within this ray-integration pipeline: the coarse network estimates sample weights, and the fine network receives additional samples biased toward regions expected to contribute to the image. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:abstract:claim:c90f7f8b0c04] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:5_2_hierarchical_volume_sampling:0:7c4cd481bcd3:claim:c7a0415d23ab] [E:arxiv:2408.03356:section:abstract:4:1447cd6be2ee:claim:6dac674e7eed]

Efficiency-oriented methods should be distinguished from the foundational formulation rather than merged into it. Baking into sparse voxel grids, polygon textures, hash or hybrid feature encodings, vector-quantized sampling, or real-time rasterization pipelines changes where features are stored, how rays or fragments are processed, and which hardware path is used. These approaches may target faster optimization, interactive rendering, lower memory, or mobile deployment, but they do not alter the definition of the original continuous MLP-based NeRF or its differentiable volume-rendering objective. [E:arxiv:2208.00277:section:abstract:1:3cd62fc6d6ab:claim:221198fa5f12] [E:arxiv:2208.00277:abstract:claim:ec4c891ab978] [E:arxiv:2311.12490:abstract:claim:e68894c18523] [E:arxiv:2310.14487:abstract:claim:7f4db429aa3b]

Task-oriented extensions likewise occupy a different axis. Methods for geometry extraction, anti-aliasing across scale, low-light capture, text or image editing, specular reflection tracing, semantic reconstruction, or architecture-agnostic processing may retain some NeRF concepts while adding supervision, priors, alternate renderers, or new data structures. For the present question, their relevant relationship is comparative: they show that the foundational representation is a coordinate-to-density-and-radiance field trained through volume compositing, not by itself a real-time engine, explicit surface model, physically complete material model, or universal editing representation. [E:arxiv:2303.09431:section:abstract:1:1957c530cb87:claim:cd42e15d6df7] [E:arxiv:2304.10075:abstract:claim:460b21afb70f] [E:arxiv:2307.10664:abstract:claim:680212073b17] [E:arxiv:2112.05139:abstract:claim:e725d479ff7b] [E:arxiv:2405.14871:abstract:claim:5e9e21d14ae9] [E:arxiv:2502.09623:abstract:claim:8ffcb6c11852]

## Representative Methods

The foundational NeRF method is a per-scene optimization problem. Its learned object is not a mesh, voxel array, or multi-view image bank, but a continuous volumetric scene function approximated by a fully connected neural network. The network receives a spatial point and a viewing direction, and returns an emitted color together with a volume density; training adjusts the network weights so that images formed by rendering this field agree with a sparse collection of posed photographs. Thus, the central mechanism has two coupled parts: a coordinate-based neural representation of local radiance and occupancy, and a differentiable renderer that turns those local quantities into full camera images. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:abstract:claim:c90f7f8b0c04] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:3_neural_radiance_field_scene_representation:0:e6a7774107f3:claim:2f4a62451a0d] At the representation level, the original paper defines a 5D vector-valued function whose conceptual input is a 3D location x=(x,y,z) and a 2D viewing direction (θ,φ), and whose output is color c=(r,g,b) and density σ. In the implemented network, direction is represented by a 3D Cartesian unit vector d. The learned mapping is written as FΘ:(x,d)→(c,σ), where Θ denotes the MLP parameters. This coordinate-based definition means the field can in principle be queried at continuous positions rather than only at fixed grid cells, although every rendered image uses a finite set of sampled queries. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:3_neural_radiance_field_scene_representation:0:e6a7774107f3:claim:2f4a62451a0d] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:3_neural_radiance_field_scene_representation:0:e6a7774107f3:claim:635a242c0596] The output dependence is deliberately asymmetric. Density σ is predicted from position x alone, making it a view-invariant scalar field that controls how strongly a spatial location absorbs or occludes light. RGB color c is allowed to depend on both x and the ray direction d, so the same occupied location can have different emitted radiance when seen from different viewpoints. This design gives NeRF a single occupancy-like field for compositing while retaining enough directional freedom to represent non-Lambertian appearance, including view-dependent highlights. It does not, however, explicitly recover separate physical material, lighting, roughness, or normal fields. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:3_neural_radiance_field_scene_representation:0:e6a7774107f3:claim:2f4a62451a0d] [E:arxiv:2306.03000:section:unknown:2:26aa95755737:claim:d216ece2b6d6] The original MLP architecture enforces that asymmetry in two stages. Eight fully connected ReLU layers, each with 256 channels, first process only the 3D position x. Their output produces the scalar density σ and a 256-dimensional intermediate feature vector. That feature vector is concatenated with the camera ray's viewing direction d and passed through one additional fully connected ReLU layer with 128 channels, which outputs the view-dependent RGB color. Consequently, position determines both occupancy and a local appearance descriptor, while the final color can be modulated by view direction. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:3_neural_radiance_field_scene_representation:0:e6a7774107f3:claim:2f4a62451a0d] A camera ray supplies the path along which the field is evaluated. For a pixel, NeRF writes the ray as r(t)=o+td, where o is the ray origin, d is the unit viewing direction, and t indexes distance along the ray. Nearby points along this ray correspond to different spatial locations that the network may report as empty, transparent, or occupied. The renderer does not look for a single surface intersection; instead it integrates color and density through the volume traversed by the ray. This volumetric view is what lets the model represent soft or layered occupancy during optimization even when the final scene appears solid. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:abstract:claim:c90f7f8b0c04] [E:arxiv:2408.03356:section:abstract:4:1447cd6be2ee:claim:6dac674e7eed] The continuous rendering model assigns color to a ray by integrating emitted color weighted by density and accumulated transmittance. With σ(r(t)) as density, c(r(t),d) as directional color, and T(t) as the probability that light travels without occlusion from the near bound to t, the integral is C(r)=∫ c(r(t),d) σ(r(t)) T(t) dt, with T(t)=exp(−∫_0^t σ(r(s))ds). Higher density at a point increases that point's contribution, while earlier density reduces the contribution of points farther along the ray through exponential attenuation. [E:arxiv:2408.03356:section:abstract:4:1447cd6be2ee:claim:6dac674e7eed] Neural network queries cannot directly evaluate the continuous integral everywhere, so NeRF uses a discrete quadrature along each ray. For N samples with intervals δ_i, the density at sample i is converted to alpha opacity α_i=1−exp(−σ_iδ_i). The transmittance accumulated before that sample is T_i=exp(−Σ_{j<i}σ_jδ_j), equivalently the product of prior (1−α_j) terms. The rendered ray color is the weighted sum Ĉ(r)=Σ_i T_i(1−exp(−σ_iδ_i))c_i=Σ_i T_iα_ic_i. The quadrature treats the queried field as piecewise constant over each sampled interval. [E:arxiv:2408.03356:section:abstract:4:1447cd6be2ee:claim:6dac674e7eed] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:5_2_hierarchical_volume_sampling:0:7c4cd481bcd3:claim:c7a0415d23ab] Each weight T_iα_i has a direct rendering interpretation: it is the fraction of the ray's contribution expected to arrive from sample i after accounting for opacity in front of it. If a sample lies in free space, σ_i is near zero and α_i is near zero; if earlier samples are opaque, T_i is near zero and later samples contribute little. The sample colors c_i are therefore not averaged uniformly. They are alpha-composited from near to far, which connects the neural field to conventional volume rendering while remaining expressible with standard differentiable tensor operations. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:5_2_hierarchical_volume_sampling:0:7c4cd481bcd3:claim:c7a0415d23ab] [E:arxiv:2408.03356:section:abstract:4:1447cd6be2ee:claim:6dac674e7eed] The differentiability of this compositing rule is the key to learning NeRF from images alone, given camera poses. Sampled coordinates and directions are fed to the MLP, its colors and densities are substituted into the ray-color sum, and the resulting pixel colors are compared with ground-truth observed pixels. Gradients of the image reconstruction loss propagate through the compositing weights and color terms back to the network parameters. The original method therefore does not require 3D ground-truth density or surface labels; the photometric discrepancy between rendered and observed views supplies the training signal. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:abstract:claim:c90f7f8b0c04] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:3_neural_radiance_field_scene_representation:0:e6a7774107f3:claim:2f4a62451a0d] Raw low-dimensional coordinates tend to limit MLPs to relatively smooth functions, so foundational NeRF maps coordinates into higher-frequency sinusoidal encodings before the main network. Positional encoding is applied to spatial coordinates for the density pathway and to viewing direction where directional input enters the color pathway. Its role is to make high-frequency geometry and appearance variation easier for the network to fit. This encoding is an input transformation for the continuous MLP; it should not be confused with later explicit hash-grid, tensor, voxel, or polygon feature stores that change the underlying data structure. [E:arxiv:2306.03000:section:unknown:2:26aa95755737:claim:d216ece2b6d6] [E:arxiv:2211.15977:abstract:claim:c6d4c4258c8e] Uniform quadrature can be wasteful because many samples fall in free space or behind opaque content. The original NeRF therefore trains a coarse network and a fine network rather than relying on one uniform sample set. The coarse pass uses N_c stratified samples along the ray, evaluates them with the same volume-rendering equation, and forms sample weights w_i=T_i(1−exp(−σ_iδ_i)). After normalizing these weights, NeRF treats them as a piecewise-constant probability distribution over ray distance and uses inverse transform sampling to draw N_f additional samples in regions expected to affect the image. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:5_2_hierarchical_volume_sampling:0:7c4cd481bcd3:claim:c7a0415d23ab] The fine network is then evaluated on the union of the original coarse samples and the newly drawn samples, giving N_c+N_f total queries for the final fine-ray color. The second set is biased toward visible or otherwise high-weight regions, but the retained coarse samples still cover the full ray domain. The original paper describes this as a nonuniform discretization of the integration domain, rather than as independent Monte Carlo estimates of the whole integral. Both coarse and fine rendered colors are supervised, so the coarse distribution learns to place later samples where they are useful. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:5_2_hierarchical_volume_sampling:0:7c4cd481bcd3:claim:c7a0415d23ab] The training objective follows this two-network rendering procedure. Each network renders a ray color from its own samples, and the loss sums the coarse and fine photometric error rather than supervising only the final high-quality image. In the standard real-valued color formulation, this is a sum over rays of squared error between the rendered and ground-truth RGB color, with separate terms for the coarse and fine outputs. The coarse loss is important because the sampling distribution used by the fine stage depends on the coarse network's estimated weights. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:5_2_hierarchical_volume_sampling:0:7c4cd481bcd3:claim:c7a0415d23ab] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:abstract:claim:c90f7f8b0c04] The method's contribution is therefore best understood as an end-to-end learned volume-rendering pipeline, not merely as an MLP that predicts colors. A sparse set of calibrated 2D images defines the supervision; the MLP defines a continuous field of density and directional emitted color; ray marching and quadrature define how to form pixels; and differentiable alpha compositing defines how photometric errors update the field. Positional encoding supplies high-frequency coordinate inputs, and hierarchical sampling allocates more network evaluations to parts of each ray that are likely to matter. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:abstract:claim:c90f7f8b0c04] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:3_neural_radiance_field_scene_representation:0:e6a7774107f3:claim:2f4a62451a0d] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:5_2_hierarchical_volume_sampling:0:7c4cd481bcd3:claim:c7a0415d23ab] The applicability boundary of the foundational model is narrower than its later family of extensions. It is a scene-specific representation: a separate continuous MLP is optimized for each scene from posed images, rather than a single network that directly reconstructs arbitrary unseen scenes. Its native output is density and view-dependent emitted radiance for novel-view rendering. The original formulation does not itself provide interactive rendering, an explicit level-set surface, editable semantic parts, a full bidirectional light-transport simulation, or a real-time mobile graphics pipeline; those goals motivate later architectures and extensions. [E:arxiv:2306.03000:section:unknown:2:26aa95755737:claim:d216ece2b6d6] [E:arxiv:2208.00277:section:abstract:1:3cd62fc6d6ab:claim:221198fa5f12] [E:arxiv:2303.09431:section:abstract:1:1957c530cb87:claim:cd42e15d6df7] [E:arxiv:2405.14871:abstract:claim:5e9e21d14ae9] The computational cost follows directly from the rendering mechanism. Every pixel requires a ray, every ray requires many point samples, and every sample requires an MLP evaluation. The original hierarchical strategy improves sample allocation but still evaluates a large neural network at many positions for each image. Later acceleration methods may bake features into sparse voxels, use polygon rasterization, introduce hash or hybrid encodings, or otherwise cache and restructure the field. Those systems can inherit NeRF's image-synthesis goal, but they are implementation or representation changes around the foundational continuous-field and volume-compositing formulation rather than prerequisites for defining it. [E:arxiv:2208.00277:section:abstract:1:3cd62fc6d6ab:claim:221198fa5f12] [E:arxiv:2208.00277:abstract:claim:ec4c891ab978] [E:arxiv:2311.12490:abstract:claim:e68894c18523] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:5_2_hierarchical_volume_sampling:0:7c4cd481bcd3:claim:c7a0415d23ab] A second boundary concerns geometry. Density is a volumetric quantity, and rendering can explain observations through soft, dense, or layered regions; a high-quality novel-view image does not necessarily imply a uniquely determined zero-thickness surface. Later mesh-extraction or geometry-normalization work addresses this ambiguity with additional objectives, constraints, or extraction procedures. Within the original NeRF explanation, σ should therefore be read as the opacity-generating field used by differentiable volume rendering, not as an explicit signed-distance function or a guaranteed reconstruction of object surfaces. [E:arxiv:2303.09431:section:abstract:1:1957c530cb87:claim:cd42e15d6df7] [E:arxiv:2303.17968:abstract:claim:f770c190e6a8] [E:arxiv:2010.07492:abstract:claim:bf4649c8548a] In summary, foundational NeRF learns FΘ(x,d)=(c,σ) per scene, with σ determined by position and c dependent on position and view. For each camera ray, it samples points r(t)=o+td, queries color and density, converts density and interval length into alpha, accumulates transmittance, and computes Ĉ(r)=Σ_iT_iα_ic_i. Since this quadrature-based renderer is differentiable, the coarse and fine MLPs are optimized by reducing the error between rendered and observed RGB images. Positional encoding and hierarchical sampling complete the original method by enabling high-frequency detail and concentrating evaluations along relevant portions of rays. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:3_neural_radiance_field_scene_representation:0:e6a7774107f3:claim:2f4a62451a0d] [E:arxiv:2408.03356:section:abstract:4:1447cd6be2ee:claim:6dac674e7eed] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:5_2_hierarchical_volume_sampling:0:7c4cd481bcd3:claim:c7a0415d23ab] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:abstract:claim:c90f7f8b0c04]

## Comparative Evidence Analysis

The experimental comparison in this review is organized by the stages that can be measured in the foundational NeRF pipeline: representation capacity, ray-sample allocation, differentiable rendering, and supervision from posed images. This is an explanatory grouping for the requested formulation, not a benchmark taxonomy from the original paper. Because the question asks for the foundational method rather than a ranking among later NeRF variants, numerical results from acceleration, anti-aliasing, editing, low-light, reflection, or mobile-rendering papers are not treated as comparable evidence for the original formulation. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:abstract:claim:c90f7f8b0c04] [E:arxiv:2306.03000:abstract:claim:342e1123f513]

The central experimental setup of foundational NeRF is per-scene optimization from a sparse set of 2D images with known camera poses. The independent object being fit is the MLP-defined field FΘ:(x,d)→(c,σ), while the measured outcome is whether images rendered from held-out camera views match real observations. There is no separate 3D density label or surface annotation in this basic setup: sampled coordinates and directions are passed through the network, volume rendering produces pixel colors, and the residual between synthesized and ground-truth images supplies gradients to Θ. Thus, the renderer is part of the training computation rather than only a post-training visualization tool. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:abstract:claim:c90f7f8b0c04] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:3_neural_radiance_field_scene_representation:0:e6a7774107f3:claim:2f4a62451a0d]

Along the representation dimension, the tested hypothesis is that a continuous coordinate-based MLP can encode both occupancy-like geometry and view-dependent appearance in one scene-specific function. The architecture separates these roles by predicting σ from x alone and c from x together with d. In the original network, eight fully connected ReLU layers with 256 channels process position and output density plus a 256-dimensional feature; concatenating that feature with the viewing direction and applying one 128-channel ReLU layer yields RGB. This supports the method's intended comparison against prior neural rendering and view-synthesis approaches: geometry need not be stored as a fixed mesh or voxel grid, and non-Lambertian color can vary with viewpoint while density remains tied to spatial location. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:3_neural_radiance_field_scene_representation:0:e6a7774107f3:claim:2f4a62451a0d] [E:arxiv:2306.03000:section:unknown:2:26aa95755737:claim:d216ece2b6d6]

The rendering comparison is between direct surface-style selection and volumetric integration. NeRF does not choose one intersection per pixel; it queries N locations along r(t)=o+td and combines their local outputs. In the discrete model, interval length δ_i and density σ_i determine α_i=1−exp(−σ_iδ_i), while T_i=exp(−Σ_{j<i}σ_jδ_j) accounts for attenuation by earlier samples. The predicted ray color is Ĉ(r)=Σ_i T_iα_ic_i. The experimentally relevant property is that all these operations are differentiable, so errors in observed RGB can change both color predictions and the density field through their effects on alpha and transmittance. [E:arxiv:2408.03356:section:abstract:4:1447cd6be2ee:claim:6dac674e7eed] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:5_2_hierarchical_volume_sampling:0:7c4cd481bcd3:claim:c7a0415d23ab]

The sampling experiment compares dense or uniform evaluation with coarse-to-fine allocation. Uniformly evaluating the network at many points is inefficient because free space and occluded regions can receive repeated queries even though they contribute little to the image. The original method therefore trains a coarse and a fine network. The coarse network is evaluated at N_c stratified samples, and its compositing weights w_i=T_i(1−exp(−σ_iδ_i)) are normalized into a piecewise-constant probability distribution over ray distance. Inverse transform sampling then draws N_f additional locations from that distribution. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:5_2_hierarchical_volume_sampling:0:7c4cd481bcd3:claim:c7a0415d23ab]

The fine-stage condition differs from the coarse-stage condition and should not be interpreted as two independent estimators competing on identical samples. NeRF evaluates the fine network on the union of the initial N_c stratified samples and the N_f samples drawn from the coarse distribution, then computes the final color with N_c+N_f samples. This biases extra computation toward regions expected to contain visible content, but the paper describes it as a nonuniform discretization of the whole ray domain, not as independent Monte Carlo estimates of the integral. Both coarse and fine outputs are supervised, which makes the coarse weights useful for later sample placement. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:5_2_hierarchical_volume_sampling:0:7c4cd481bcd3:claim:c7a0415d23ab] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:abstract:claim:c90f7f8b0c04]

The training metric in the foundational formulation is photometric error between rendered and observed ray colors, with coarse and fine terms both included. This comparison evaluates the complete chain—coordinate encoding, MLP prediction, density-to-alpha conversion, transmittance accumulation, and RGB compositing—rather than evaluating density or surface accuracy directly. Consequently, strong view-synthesis error supports the learned field's ability to explain the training images and generalize to the tested novel views, but it does not by itself establish that σ is a unique physical surface or a signed-distance function. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:abstract:claim:c90f7f8b0c04] [E:arxiv:2303.09431:section:abstract:1:1957c530cb87:claim:cd42e15d6df7]

Later systems provide useful contrast points, but their reported speed, memory, or quality numbers are not directly comparable to the original NeRF experiment unless the representation, samples, hardware, datasets, and training schedule are matched. Sparse voxel baking and polygon rasterization replace repeated MLP ray queries with cached features or standard graphics pipelines; hash, tensor, and hybrid encodings alter where scene features are stored; and multiscale or reflection methods add different representations and rendering assumptions. These comparisons identify computational and modeling trade-offs, but they do not test the same exact baseline as the original continuous-MLP and differentiable-volume-rendering formulation. [E:arxiv:2208.00277:section:abstract:1:3cd62fc6d6ab:claim:221198fa5f12] [E:arxiv:2208.00277:abstract:claim:ec4c891ab978] [E:arxiv:2211.15977:abstract:claim:c6d4c4258c8e] [E:arxiv:2311.12490:abstract:claim:e68894c18523]

The original paper reports that this pipeline achieved state-of-the-art novel-view synthesis for complex scenes in its study and outperformed prior neural rendering and view-synthesis work; the available source excerpts do not provide a complete matched table of datasets, metrics, baselines, and numerical scores, so no numerical ranking should be reconstructed here. The evidence that is directly supported at the formulation level is methodological: posed 2D images are sufficient supervision because ray compositing is differentiable, position-only density plus directional color provides the intended multiview consistency and appearance flexibility, and hierarchical sampling targets network evaluations toward samples with greater expected visual contribution. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:abstract:claim:c90f7f8b0c04] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:3_neural_radiance_field_scene_representation:0:e6a7774107f3:claim:2f4a62451a0d] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:5_2_hierarchical_volume_sampling:0:7c4cd481bcd3:claim:c7a0415d23ab]

Accordingly, the appropriate conclusion from this experiment-focused explanation is not a cross-family benchmark ranking. Under the foundational NeRF setting, the validated mechanism is an end-to-end per-scene fit: sample camera rays, query a continuous 5D neural field, convert local density and color into alpha-weighted transmittance composites, and optimize coarse and fine MLPs against observed RGB images. Claims about interactive frame rates, mobile deployment, memory reduction, robust geometry extraction, anti-aliasing, or physically complete reflections require the separate methods and matched experiments associated with those later systems and cannot be inferred from the original formulation alone. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:abstract:claim:c90f7f8b0c04] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:5_2_hierarchical_volume_sampling:0:7c4cd481bcd3:claim:c7a0415d23ab] [E:arxiv:2208.00277:section:abstract:1:3cd62fc6d6ab:claim:221198fa5f12] [E:arxiv:2303.09431:section:abstract:1:1957c530cb87:claim:cd42e15d6df7]

## Limitations and Open Problems

The main open limitation of foundational NeRF is computational rather than merely implementational. Rendering a pixel requires marching a camera ray through the scene, evaluating a large MLP at hundreds of sampled positions, and integrating density and radiance from those queries; the original hierarchical sampler reduces wasted samples but does not remove this many-query-per-pixel structure. As a result, the basic formulation is poorly matched to interactive visualization, especially when high resolution or many views must be rendered. Later acceleration systems address this by baking sparse voxel features, using polygon rasterization, or replacing plain MLP storage with hash grids, tensors, or hybrid encodings, which shows that speed is a separate design objective from defining the continuous radiance field. [E:arxiv:2208.00277:section:abstract:1:3cd62fc6d6ab:claim:221198fa5f12] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:5_2_hierarchical_volume_sampling:0:7c4cd481bcd3:claim:c7a0415d23ab] [E:arxiv:2211.15977:abstract:claim:c6d4c4258c8e] [E:arxiv:2208.00277:abstract:claim:ec4c891ab978] The acceleration trade-off is not free. Caching a NeRF into explicit data structures can improve rendering speed, but it increases memory use; for example, SNeRG's sparse volumetric textures are described as requiring substantial GPU memory, which prevents deployment on common mobile devices. MobileNeRF instead moves the deferred view-dependent decode into a small shader-stage MLP behind textured polygons so standard z-buffer rasterization can exploit commodity GPU parallelism. These systems demonstrate that the foundational MLP's compact functional description and later real-time data structures optimize different points in the compute, memory, and hardware-compatibility space. [E:arxiv:2208.00277:section:abstract:1:3cd62fc6d6ab:claim:221198fa5f12] [E:arxiv:2208.00277:abstract:claim:ec4c891ab978] [E:arxiv:2208.00277:section:abstract:1:3cd62fc6d6ab:claim:b6838ad1372c]

A second open problem is geometric ambiguity. The photometric renderer only needs a volume whose alpha-composited colors explain the observed images; it does not require a unique zero-thickness surface. NeRF can therefore use dense, soft, or layered occupancy to approximate complex appearance and geometry, and a high-quality rendered view does not uniquely determine a mesh. NeRF++ explicitly identifies a shape-radiance ambiguity in radiance fields, while later mesh-extraction work notes that radiance fields optimized for novel view synthesis are commonly not explicit level-set surfaces and may rely on transparency or layering. Consequently, density σ should not automatically be interpreted as a signed-distance field or as a guaranteed surface reconstruction. [E:arxiv:2010.07492:abstract:claim:bf4649c8548a] [E:arxiv:2303.09431:section:abstract:1:1957c530cb87:claim:cd42e15d6df7] [E:arxiv:2303.17968:abstract:claim:f770c190e6a8] View-dependent color intensifies this geometry problem under non-Lambertian or changing-light conditions. Allowing color to depend on viewing direction is essential for representing specular and other directional appearance in the original model, but it also gives the network capacity to explain image variation through radiance rather than invariant geometry. VDN-NeRF states that shape-radiance ambiguity remains inevitable and proposes view-dependence normalization to reduce its effect on geometry without changing the volume-rendering pipeline. This supports a bounded conclusion: the foundational representation is directly suited to image synthesis, but accurate geometry extraction may require additional constraints, normalization, or extraction methods. [E:arxiv:2303.17968:abstract:claim:f770c190e6a8] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:3_neural_radiance_field_scene_representation:0:e6a7774107f3:claim:2f4a62451a0d] [E:arxiv:2306.03000:section:unknown:2:26aa95755737:claim:d216ece2b6d6]

The basic model also lacks an explicit multiscale or anti-aliasing model. A conventional NeRF query is associated with a point along a ray, whereas a pixel or ray sample can cover a conical region whose footprint changes with distance and image resolution. Mip-NeRF addresses scale by using a conical frustum and integrated positional encoding, but that MLP-based approach is described as suitable for offline rendering; Mip-VoG instead introduces explicit multiscale voxel grids and a deferred architecture for real-time anti-aliasing. The relevant limitation for foundational NeRF is therefore concrete: training images at nonuniform scales can lead to blur, and distant or zoomed-out test views can produce aliasing because the original point-query formulation does not encode the sample's scale footprint. [E:arxiv:2304.10075:abstract:claim:460b21afb70f] [E:arxiv:2304.10075:abstract:claim:fbd225b1e889] [E:arxiv:2304.10075:abstract:claim:ad41d048e649]

Specular reflections reveal another modeling boundary. Directional emitted color lets a point change appearance with the outgoing viewing direction, but the original field does not trace incoming reflection paths or separate nearby reflected content from the material response. Later ray-traced NeRF work reports that prior methods can improve detailed specular appearance from distant environment illumination but cannot consistently synthesize reflections of closer content, and that expensive neural outgoing-radiance networks also limit optimization and rendering speed. Thus, view-dependent RGB in foundational NeRF is a phenomenological radiance output, not a complete bidirectional reflection or global-illumination simulation. [E:arxiv:2405.14871:abstract:claim:5e9e21d14ae9] [E:arxiv:2405.14871:abstract:claim:8c78d9808e63] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:3_neural_radiance_field_scene_representation:0:e6a7774107f3:claim:2f4a62451a0d]

The original representation is scene-specific and optimization-based. A separate neural continuous volume is fitted to each scene from posed images, and the training signal depends on known camera poses and a photometric rendering loss. This is effective for per-scene novel view synthesis, but it differs from training a single model to reconstruct arbitrary unseen scenes and from architectures designed for downstream inference across many NeRF families. The selected sources do not establish a universal numerical training-cost gap across all later methods; they do show that subsequent work targets faster per-scene distillation, explicit feature encodings, and architecture-agnostic processing as separate needs. [E:arxiv:2306.03000:section:unknown:2:26aa95755737:claim:d216ece2b6d6] [E:arxiv:2211.15977:abstract:claim:c6d4c4258c8e] [E:arxiv:2211.15977:abstract:claim:43c5ef6752a5] [E:arxiv:2502.09623:abstract:claim:557d0ba8c7ed] Representation choice also affects downstream controllability. Plain MLPs, sparse tensors, low-rank tensors, hash tables, and composite structures have different trade-offs; PVD specifically notes that hash-table-based representations train and render quickly but lack clear geometric meaning, which hampers spatial-relation-aware editing. This means that replacing the foundational MLP solely for speed can make manipulation or semantic interpretation harder, while converting representations after training may be needed to match a downstream task. The limitation is therefore not a simple ranking among backbones: rendering speed, training speed, memory, geometric interpretability, and editability can conflict. [E:arxiv:2211.15977:abstract:claim:c6d4c4258c8e] [E:arxiv:2211.15977:abstract:claim:43c5ef6752a5] [E:arxiv:2211.15977:abstract:claim:c78226efe27c]

Integration with conventional graphics pipelines is another unresolved issue for the native model. Foundational NeRF relies on specialized volumetric ray marching rather than the meshes and z-buffered rasterization used by most standard graphics pipelines. Later polygon-based and Unreal Engine integrations explicitly introduce textured polygons, optimized geometry, levels of detail, or engine rasterization to obtain interactive and 4K rendering workflows. These systems indicate that the original continuous volume is not directly equivalent to an asset format for standard engines, physics simulation, or hardware-accelerated polygon pipelines. [E:arxiv:2303.09431:section:abstract:1:1957c530cb87:claim:cd42e15d6df7] [E:arxiv:2208.00277:abstract:claim:ec4c891ab978] [E:arxiv:2208.00277:abstract:claim:aba04be0da10] [E:arxiv:2310.13263:abstract:claim:e5f57fea071a]

Finally, the open problems should be scoped to the foundational formulation rather than generalized as failures of the entire NeRF family. Slow ray-sampled MLP evaluation, memory-heavy baking, nonunique volumetric geometry, scale aliasing, incomplete reflection physics, scene-specific fitting, and limited conventional-pipeline integration are supported limitations or trade-offs in the cited methods. They motivate later encodings, renderers, priors, geometry constraints, and task-specific extensions, but they do not by themselves establish that every later NeRF variant shares the same limitation. For the requested topic, the central boundary remains that NeRF's differentiable volume renderer provides an image-driven learning rule, not a universal solution to real-time rendering, exact reconstruction, material inference, editing, or graphics-engine interoperability. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:abstract:claim:c90f7f8b0c04] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:5_2_hierarchical_volume_sampling:0:7c4cd481bcd3:claim:c7a0415d23ab] [E:arxiv:2208.00277:section:abstract:1:3cd62fc6d6ab:claim:221198fa5f12] [E:arxiv:2303.09431:section:abstract:1:1957c530cb87:claim:cd42e15d6df7]

## Conclusion

The core answer is that NeRF is not a mesh or discrete voxel model, but a coordinate-based neural volume FΘ(x,d)=(c,σ), rendered through quadrature of the volume-rendering integral: Ĉ(r)=Σ_i T_iα_i c_i, with α_i=1−exp(−σ_iδ_i). This formulation connects local density and directional radiance to supervised pixels through differentiable transmittance-weighted compositing. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:abstract:claim:c90f7f8b0c04] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:3_neural_radiance_field_scene_representation:0:e6a7774107f3:claim:2f4a62451a0d] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:3_neural_radiance_field_scene_representation:0:e6a7774107f3:claim:635a242c0596] [E:arxiv:2408.03356:section:abstract:4:1447cd6be2ee:claim:6dac674e7eed] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:5_2_hierarchical_volume_sampling:0:7c4cd481bcd3:claim:c7a0415d23ab]

Its main trade-off is expressive image formation against scope and cost: position-only density supplies multiview-consistent occupancy, view-dependent color represents non-Lambertian appearance, and hierarchical sampling improves query allocation, but the native model remains per-scene, requires many MLP evaluations per ray, and does not itself guarantee explicit surfaces, real-time rendering, material decomposition, anti-aliasing, reflection tracing, editing, or graphics-engine interoperability. claim_records.text: RayGauss achieves inference speeds of 25 FPS on the Blender dataset.

RayGauss provides a physically consistent formulation of emitted radiance c and density σ, decomposed with Gaussian functions associated with Spherical Gaussians/Harmonics for all-frequency colorimetric representation.
RayGauss introduces a method enabling differentiable ray casting of irregularly distributed Gaussians using an algorithm that integrates radiance fields slab by slab and leverages a BVH structure.

fact_fields.method: Differentiable slab-by-slab ray casting with BVH

claim_records.text: RayGauss achieves superior rendering quality compared to the state-of-the-art while maintaining reasonable training times.
RayGauss represents radiance fields as a weighted sum of locally supported elliptical basis functions with optimizable positions, orientations, and scales.

fact_fields.method: Elliptical basis function radiance field representation

claim_records.text: RayGauss combines spherical harmonics (SH) and spherical Gaussians (SG) with elliptical basis functions to represent high-frequency color variations such as specular reflections.
RayGauss uses volume ray casting which produces high-quality images with fewer simplifications than splatting-based methods like 3D Gaussian Splatting.
Splatting algorithms cause artifacts when deviating from training views, such as flickering due to a sudden change in primitives ordering.
RayGauss's ray casting algorithm sequentially integrates the radiance field slab-by-slab, accumulating colorimetric properties along the ray in slabs of space corresponding to multiple samples.
RayGauss implements its ray casting algorithm and backpropagation on GPU using a Bounding Volume Hierarchy (BVH) with the OptiX library.
The classic volumetric rendering equation used in NeRF and 3D Gaussian Splatting is C(r) = ∫ c(r(t), d)σ(r(t))T(t) dt, where T(t) = exp(-∫σ(r(s)) ds).

claim_records.text: NeRFMeshing proposes a compact and flexible architecture that enables easy 3D surface reconstruction from any NeRF-driven approach.
NeRFMeshing distills the volumetric 3D representation of a trained radiance field into a Signed Surface Approximation Network, allowing easy extraction of the 3D mesh and appearance.
NeRFMeshing's final 3D mesh is physically accurate and can be rendered in real time on an array of devices.
NeRFs are optimized for view synthesis and do not enforce an accurate underlying geometry on the radiance field.
NeRFMeshing produces meshes with neural colors having accurate geometry that can be rendered in real time on commodity hardware.
SSAN estimates a Truncated Signed Distance Field (TSDF) and a feature appearance field.
NeRFMeshing can be leveraged together with any NeRF, enabling easy incorporation of new advances such as improved handling of unbounded scenes or reflective objects.
NeRFMeshing extracts meshes from scenes including Chair, Hot-dog, Lego (Blender dataset) and Garden (MipNeRF 360 dataset).

NeRF methods often rely on layering and transparency effects to approximate complex appearance and geometry, approximating object surfaces by dense regions of the volume instead of surfaces of zero thickness.
NeRFMeshing does not rely on a fixed grid template during training, enabling reconstruction at any arbitrary resolution afterwards.
NeRFMeshing relies on NeRF networks trained from images, without requiring additional supervision signals such as depth.

claim_records.text: The NeRF method optimizes an underlying continuous volumetric scene function using a sparse set of input views to synthesize novel views of complex scenes.

The NeRF scene representation uses a fully-connected non-convolutional deep network that takes a single continuous 5D coordinate (spatial location (x,y,z) and viewing direction (theta, phi)) as input and outputs volume density and view-dependent emitted radiance at that location.

fact_fields.method: fully-connected non-convolutional deep network scene representation

claim_records.text: NeRF synthesizes views by querying 5D coordinates along camera rays and using classic volume rendering techniques to project output colors and densities into an image.
Because volume rendering is naturally differentiable, the only input required to optimize the NeRF representation is a set of images with known camera poses.
The NeRF method outperforms prior work on neural rendering and view synthesis for rendering photorealistic novel views of scenes with complicated geometry and appearance.
The volume density σ(x) in NeRF can be interpreted as the differential probability of a ray terminating at an infinitesimal particle at location x.

The expected color C(r) of a camera ray r(t) = o + td with near and far bounds tn and tf is computed via the integral C(r) = ∫ from tn to tf of T(t)σ(r(t))c(r(t), d)dt, where T(t) = exp(−∫ from tn to t of σ(r(s))ds).
The function T(t) denotes the accumulated transmittance along the ray from tn to t, i.e., the probability that the ray travels from tn to t without hitting any other particle.
Rendering a view from the continuous neural radiance field requires estimating the integral C(r) for a camera ray traced through each pixel of the desired virtual camera.
The NeRF MLP FΘ first processes the input 3D coordinate x with 8 fully-connected layers using ReLU activations and 256 channels per layer, and outputs σ and a 256-dimensional feature vector.

The 256-dimensional feature vector output by the initial 8 layers is concatenated with the camera ray's viewing direction and passed to one additional fully-connected layer using ReLU activation and 128 channels that outputs the view-dependent RGB color.

The NeRF representation encourages multiview consistency by restricting the network to predict volume density σ as a function of only location x, while allowing RGB color c to be predicted as a function of both location and viewing direction.

NeRF approximates the continuous 5D scene representation with an MLP network FΘ: (x, d) → (c, σ) and optimizes its weights Θ to map from each input 5D coordinate to its corresponding volume density and directional emitted color.

The hierarchical volume sampling approach simultaneously optimizes two networks: one coarse network and one fine network, to increase rendering efficiency by allocating samples proportionally to their expected effect on the final rendering.

In hierarchical volume sampling, a set of Nc locations is first sampled using stratified sampling and evaluated by the coarse network; the output of the coarse network is then used to produce a more informed sampling of points along each ray biased towards relevant parts of the volume.

Normalizing the coarse network weights as ŵi = wi / sum_{j=1 to Nc} wj produces a piecewise-constant PDF along the ray, from which a second set of Nf locations is sampled using inverse transform sampling.

fact_fields.method: inverse transform sampling from piecewise-constant PDF

claim_records.text: The fine network is evaluated at the union of the first Nc and second Nf sample sets, and the final rendered color of the ray Ĉf(r) is computed using all Nc+Nf samples.

The hierarchical sampling procedure addresses a similar goal as importance sampling, but uses sampled values as a nonuniform discretization of the whole integration domain rather than treating each sample as an independent probabilistic estimate of the entire integral.

Two improvements are introduced to enable NeRF to represent high-resolution complex scenes: positional encoding of input coordinates to assist the MLP in representing high-frequency functions, and a hierarchical sampling procedure to efficiently sample this high-frequency representation.
Having the network FΘ directly operate on xyzθφ input coordinates results in renderings that perform poorly at representing high-frequency variation in color and geometry.
Reformulating FΘ as a composition of two functions FΘ = F'Θ ◦ γ, where γ is a fixed mapping from R into a higher dimensional space R^{2L} and F'Θ is a regular MLP, significantly improves performance.

The encoding function γ(p) = (sin(2^0 πp), cos(2^0 πp), ..., sin(2^{L−1} πp), cos(2^{L−1} πp)) is applied separately to each of the three coordinate values in x (normalized to lie in [−1, 1]) and to the three components of the Cartesian viewing direction unit vector d (which lie in [−1, 1]).
In NeRF experiments, L = 10 is used for the positional encoding γ(x) of spatial coordinates, and L = 4 is used for the positional encoding γ(d) of viewing directions.

The hierarchical volume sampling approach simultaneously optimizes two networks: one coarse network and one fine network, to increase rendering efficiency by allocating samples proportionally to their expected effect on the final rendering.

In hierarchical volume sampling, a set of Nc locations is first sampled using stratified sampling and evaluated by the coarse network; the output of the coarse network is then used to produce a more informed sampling of points along each ray biased towards relevant parts of the volume.

Normalizing the coarse network weights as ŵi = wi / sum_{j=1 to Nc} wj produces a piecewise-constant PDF along the ray, from which a second set of Nf locations is sampled using inverse transform sampling.
The fine network is evaluated at the union of the first Nc and second Nf sample sets, and the final rendered color of the ray Ĉf(r) is computed using all Nc+Nf samples.

The hierarchical sampling procedure addresses a similar goal as importance sampling, but uses sampled values as a nonuniform discretization of the whole integration domain rather than treating each sample as an independent probabilistic estimate of the entire integral.

Two improvements are introduced to enable NeRF to represent high-resolution complex scenes: positional encoding of input coordinates to assist the MLP in representing high-frequency functions, and a hierarchical sampling procedure to efficiently sample this high-frequency representation.
Having the network FΘ directly operate on xyzθφ input coordinates results in renderings that perform poorly at representing high-frequency variation in color and geometry.
Reformulating FΘ as a composition of two functions FΘ = F'Θ ◦ γ, where γ is a fixed mapping from R into a higher dimensional space R^{2L} and F'Θ is a regular MLP, significantly improves performance.

The encoding function γ(p) = (sin(2^0 πp), cos(2^0 πp), ..., sin(2^{L−1} πp), cos(2^{L−1} πp)) is applied separately to each of the three coordinate values in x (normalized to lie in [−1, 1]) and to the three components of the Cartesian viewing direction unit vector d (which lie in [−1, 1]).
In NeRF experiments, L = 10 is used for the positional encoding γ(x) of spatial coordinates, and L = 4 is used for the positional encoding γ(d) of viewing directions.

claim_records.text: Traditional NeRFs rely upon specialized volumetric rendering algorithms based on ray marching that are mismatched to the capabilities of widely deployed graphics hardware.
MobileNeRF represents the NeRF as a set of polygons with textures representing binary opacities and feature vectors, enabling novel image synthesis with standard rendering pipelines.

Traditional rendering of the MobileNeRF polygons with a z-buffer yields an image with features at every pixel, which are interpreted by a small, view-dependent MLP running in a fragment shader to produce a final pixel color.

fact_fields.method: z-buffer polygon rasterization + fragment shader MLP

claim_records.text: The MobileNeRF approach enables NeRFs to be rendered with the traditional polygon rasterization pipeline, which provides massive pixel-level parallelism, achieving interactive frame rates on a wide range of compute platforms, including mobile phones.

Traditional NeRF implementations use a volumetric rendering algorithm that evaluates a large MLP at hundreds of sample positions along the ray for each pixel in order to estimate and integrate density and radiance.
The traditional NeRF volumetric rendering process is far too slow for interactive visualization.
SNeRG (Sparse Neural Radiance Grids) precomputation and deferred rendering approach increases the rendering speed of NeRF by three orders of magnitude.

SNeRG still relies upon ray marching through a sparse voxel grid to produce the features for each pixel, and thus cannot fully utilize the parallelism available in commodity graphics processing units (GPUs).
SNeRG requires a significant amount of GPU memory to store the volumetric textures, which prohibits it from running on common mobile devices.
MobileNeRF's rendering pipeline does not sample rays or sort polygons in depth order, and thus can model only binary opacities.
MobileNeRF is 10× faster than SNeRG with the same output quality on standard test scenes.

fact_fields.method: MobileNeRF vs SNeRG rendering speed comparison

claim_records.text: MobileNeRF consumes less memory by storing surface textures instead of volumetric textures, enabling the method to run on integrated GPUs with limited memory and power.
MobileNeRF runs on a web browser and is compatible with all devices tested, as its viewer is an HTML webpage.
MobileNeRF allows real-time manipulation of reconstructed objects/scenes, as they are simple triangle meshes.
MobileNeRF does not need reconstructed 3D geometry as input.

NVDiffRec combines differentiable marching tetrahedra with differentiable rasterization to perform full inverse rendering and extract triangle meshes, materials, and lighting from images, but incurs a significant loss in view-synthesis quality.
While real-time rendering is possible with simple lighting using NVDiffRec, global illumination (GI) is computationally infeasible on mobile hardware.
MobileNeRF simply caches the outgoing radiance, which does not need expensive compute to model GI effects, and also results in higher view-synthesis quality.
Rendering a NeRF involves evaluating a large neural network at multiple 3D locations per pixel, preventing real-time rendering.

claim_records.text: Progressive Volume Distillation (PVD) is a systematic distillation method that enables any-to-any conversions between different NeRF architectures, including MLP, sparse or low-rank tensors, hashtables and their compositions.

With PVD, an MLP-based NeRF model can be distilled from a hashtable-based Instant-NGP model at a 10×~20× faster speed than training the original NeRF from scratch, while achieving a superior level of synthesis quality.
PVD performs distillation progressively on different levels of volume representations, from shallower to deeper, to enable fast architecture conversions.
PVD employs special treatment of density to address its specific numerical instability problem during distillation.
Empirical validation of PVD is conducted on the NeRF-Synthetic, LLFF and TanksAndTemples datasets.

A NeRF model distilled by PVD from an INGP teacher within 1.5 hours achieves improved synthesis quality compared to a NeRF model trained from scratch using 25 hours on the Family and Barn scenes from the TanksAndTemples dataset.
Hashtable-based NeRF representations admit faster training and rendering but their lack of clear geometric meaning hampers downstream tasks like spatial-relation-aware editing.

PVD uses a block-wise distillation strategy to accelerate training based on a unified view of different NeRF architectures, and employs special treatment of the dynamic density volume range by clipping to improve training stability and synthesis quality.
Distillation from hashtable and VM-decomposition structures often helps boost student model synthesis quality and consumes less time than training from scratch.
PVD enables downstream applications to optimally adapt neural NeRF representations for a given task in a post hoc fashion.

claim_records.text: NeRF generates a volumetric representation called a radiance field that is capable of creating color and density for every point within the relevant 3D space, rather than directly restoring the whole 3D scene geometry.
NeRF uses an interpolation approach to produce new 3D reconstructed views of complicated scenes from 2D images.

CAMPARI simultaneously learns a camera generator and an image generator, enabling use of complex camera distributions without manual tuning, and represents scenes through foreground and background decomposition for 3D-consistent representations and accurate camera distribution recovery.
CAMPARI surpasses baseline models that heavily depend on accurately matched camera distributions, due to its performance without camera parameter tuning.
CAMPARI faces the challenge of generating inward-facing faces compared to the traditional hollow face illusion where convex faces appear concave.
Pix2NeRF introduces a pipeline to generate NeRF from a single input image, built upon π-GAN which maps latent codes to radiance fields.
Pix2NeRF employs an unsupervised approach and can be trained with independent images, with potential applications in 3D avatar generation, novel view synthesis, and super-resolution.
A limitation of Pix2NeRF is its current restriction to work with only one category per dataset, impeding its ability to generalize to new categories.
Pix2NeRF is built on top of π-GAN but is not limited to using π-GAN as its backbone; newer generative NeRF models such as EG3D may achieve better visual quality if used as a backbone.

NeRF uses a deep neural network to represent complex scenes in a fully connected, non-convolutional way, with input as a continuous 5D coordinate and output as volume density and view-dependent emitted radiance at that spatial location.
The 5D coordinate space in NeRF includes three dimensions for spatial coordinates (x,y,z) and two dimensions for camera viewing angles (θ,φ).
NeRF uses classic volume rendering techniques to synthesize views and is optimized using a set of images with known camera poses.
NeRF introduces positional encoding and a hierarchical sampling strategy to address the inefficiency of the basic implementation.
Using input viewing direction, NeRF can represent non-Lambertian effects such as specularities.
NeRF uses a separate neural continuous volume representation network for each scene.

claim_records.text: The introduced single-view volumetric field reconstruction technique models unknown volumetric field distributions using an unconditional diffusion model trained on a benchmark dataset of 1,000 synthetically simulated volumetric density fields.

fact_fields.method: unconditional diffusion model for single-view volumetric field reconstruction

claim_records.text: The neural diffusion model for volumetric field reconstruction is trained on the latent codes of a novel, diffusion-friendly monoplanar representation.
A physically-based differentiable volume renderer is employed to provide gradients with respect to light transport in the latent space for the volumetric reconstruction pipeline.

The reconstruction of internal density distribution of highly dense volumes is widely considered nearly impossible due to high uncertainty in the light scattering process and presence of vanishing gradients, and this limitation can only be alleviated by incorporating prior information during reconstruction.

The proposed approach employs a diffusion prior to guide a Physically-based Differentiable Volume Renderer (PDVR) toward reconstructing a plausible volumetric field, by considering the gradient of the image loss with respect to the learned latent space representation to control variations in the diffusion step.

fact_fields.method: diffusion prior guided Physically-based Differentiable Volume Renderer (PDVR)

claim_records.text: The diffusion model for volumetric reconstruction is trained on a dataset of 1,000 synthetically simulated cumulus cloud volumetric density fields, using a novel diffusion-friendly representation for decoding.

The renderer is coupled with the diffusion model to reconstruct radiance parameters using the prior for the density distribution but not for its appearance, so the 3D density field can be trained solely on the prior without requiring images of all possible backgrounds and light scattering effects.
The work contributes a large database of 3D cumulus cloud-like density fields generated using numerical fluid simulation.
The work contributes a 3D cloud decoder utilizing a novel diffusion-friendly monoplanar representation, trained jointly on a subset of the cumulus cloud density field database.

The work proposes a novel Parametric Diffusion Posterior Sampling (PDPS) technique utilizing a shape-centric prior with a physically-based differentiable volume renderer, and is the first approach that integrates an unconditional diffusion model trained on volumetric density distributions with a differentiable volume renderer.
The proposed approach demonstrates potential across tasks including single- and multi-view reconstruction, and volume super-resolution.

claim_records.text: Hyb-NeRF is a neural radiance field with multi-resolution hybrid encoding that represents scenes using different encoding strategies from coarse-to-fine resolution levels: memory-efficient learnable positional features at coarse resolutions, and fast-optimizing hash-based feature grids with local details at fine resolutions.
Cone tracing-based features are embedded in the learnable positional encoding of Hyb-NeRF to eliminate encoding ambiguity and reduce aliasing artifacts.

fact_fields.method: cone tracing-based feature embedding in learnable positional encoding

claim_records.text: Extensive experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets show Hyb-NeRF achieves faster rendering speed, better rendering quality, and lower memory footprint compared to previous state-of-the-art methods.
On the ficus scene in Blender, Hyb-NeRF with 16.4M parameters achieves 35.85 PSNR and 0.986 SSIM, while JNGP with 24.4M parameters achieves 33.23 PSNR and 0.981 SSIM.

fact_fields.method: quantitative comparison on Blender ficus scene

claim_records.text: Hyb-NeRF's multi-resolution hybrid encoding concatenates coarse-level learnable positional features and fine-level hash-based dense grids of trainable features to represent input position x, resulting in a significantly lower memory footprint and higher quality representation of synthetic and real-world scenes.
All Hyb-NeRF models can reconstruct high-quality radiance fields in 9 minutes.

Hyb-NeRF's smallest model with 8.4M trainable parameters takes 4 minutes to achieve better rendering quality than state-of-the-art methods while requiring substantially less memory than previous and concurrent voxel-based methods.

claim_records.text: NeRF yields blurred rendering results when the training images are captured at non-uniform scales.
NeRF produces aliasing artifacts if the test images are taken in distant views.
Mip-NeRF's multiscale conical frustum representation is only suitable for offline rendering since it relies on integrated positional encoding (IPE) to query a multilayer perceptron (MLP).
Mip-VoG is an explicit multiscale representation with a deferred architecture designed for real-time anti-aliasing rendering.
Mip-VoG uses a density Mip-VoG for scene geometry and a feature Mip-VoG paired with a small MLP for view-dependent color.
Mip-VoG encodes scene scale using the level of detail (LOD) derived from ray differentials.
Mip-VoG uses quadrilinear interpolation to map a queried 3D location to its features and density from two neighboring downsampled voxel grids.
Mip-VoG is the first approach to offer multiscale training and real-time anti-aliasing rendering simultaneously.
Experiments on multiscale datasets show that Mip-VoG outperforms state-of-the-art real-time rendering baselines.

claim_records.text: NeRF and its variants require a lengthy training time ranging from hours to days for a single scene.
The presented voxel grid optimization approach achieves NeRF-comparable quality and converges rapidly from scratch in less than 15 minutes with a single GPU.
The voxel grid optimization representation consists of a density voxel grid for scene geometry and a feature voxel grid with a shallow network for complex view-dependent appearance.
Post-activation interpolation on voxel density is capable of producing sharp surfaces in lower grid resolution.
Direct voxel density optimization is prone to suboptimal geometry solutions, so the optimization process is robustified by imposing several priors.

Evaluation on five inward-facing benchmarks shows that the voxel grid optimization method matches, if not surpasses, NeRF's quality, while taking about 15 minutes to train from scratch for a new scene.

claim_records.text: Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) have low rendering efficiency because rendering a single pixel requires multiple network forwardings.

Existing methods to improve NeRF either reduce the number of required samples or optimize implementation to accelerate network forwarding, but the multiple sampling problem persists due to the intrinsic representation of radiance fields.
Neural Light Fields (NeLF) reduce NeRF computation cost by querying only one single network forwarding per pixel.
Existing NeLF methods require significantly larger network capacities to achieve visual quality close to NeRF, which limits their rendering efficiency in practice.
The proposed Neural Radiance Distribution Field (NeRDF) uses a small network similar to NeRF while preserving rendering speed with a single network forwarding per pixel as in NeLF.
NeRDF models the radiance distribution along each ray with frequency basis, predicts frequency weights using the network, and computes pixel values via volume rendering on radiance distributions.
NeRDF achieves approximately 254x speed-up over NeRF with similar network size, with only a marginal performance decline.

claim_records.text: Implicit neural representation methodologies have inherent computational complexity that constrains attainable frame rates and resolutions in practical applications.
VQ-NeRF reduces the sampling space of NeRF to a lower resolution and reinstates it to the original size using a pre-trained VAE decoder to mitigate the sampling time bottleneck during rendering.
Reconstructing fine texture details of the scene remains challenging with VQ-NeRF's codebook features due to high compression rates.
VQ-NeRF uses a multi-scale NeRF sampling scheme that concurrently optimizes the NeRF model at both compressed and original scales to enhance preservation of fine details.
VQ-NeRF incorporates a semantic loss function to improve geometric fidelity and semantic coherence of 3D reconstructions.
Evaluation on the DTU, BlendMVS, and H3DS datasets confirms VQ-NeRF's superior performance in achieving the optimal trade-off between rendering quality and efficiency.

claim_records.text: Meshes offer high precision for 3D representation, but their dense vertex data complicates editing.
NeRFs deliver excellent rendering quality, but suffer from structural ambiguity that hinders animation and manipulation.

The proposed 3D Hierarchical Proxy Node representation represents an object's shape and texture via a sparse set of hierarchically organized (tree-structured) proxy nodes distributed on its surface and interior.
Each proxy node stores local shape and texture information implicitly encoded by a small MLP within its neighborhood.
Querying any 3D coordinate's properties involves efficient neural interpolation and lightweight decoding from relevant nearby and parent nodes.
The HPR3D framework yields a highly compact representation where nodes align with local semantics, enabling direct drag-and-edit manipulation and offering scalable quality-complexity control.
Extensive experiments across 3D reconstruction and editing demonstrate the HPR3D method's expressive efficiency, high-fidelity rendering quality, and superior editability.

claim_records.text: Neural Radiance Fields typically struggle to reconstruct and render highly specular objects whose appearance varies quickly with changes in viewpoint.
Recent prior NeRF works can render detailed specular appearance of distant environment illumination, but are unable to synthesize consistent reflections of closer content.
Existing improved NeRF specular rendering techniques rely on large computationally-expensive neural networks to model outgoing radiance, which severely limits optimization and rendering speed.

The NeRF-Casting model casts reflection rays from points along each camera ray and traces them through the NeRF representation to render feature vectors which are decoded into color using a small inexpensive network, instead of querying an expensive neural network for outgoing view-dependent radiance at those points.
The NeRF-Casting model outperforms prior methods for view synthesis of scenes containing shiny objects.
NeRF-Casting is the only existing NeRF method that can synthesize photorealistic specular appearance and reflections in real-world scenes.
NeRF-Casting requires comparable optimization time to current state-of-the-art view synthesis models.

claim_records.text: Rendering a single pixel in NeRF requires querying the NeRF network hundreds of times.
Rendering a pixel in Neural Light Field (NeLF) amounts to one single forward pass without ray-marching.
The proposed method uses a deep residual MLP network with 88 layers to effectively learn the light field.
Sufficient data is obtained for training the deep NeLF network by transferring knowledge from a pre-trained NeRF model via data distillation.
On synthetic scenes, the proposed method achieves 26-35x FLOPs reduction per camera ray compared to NeRF.
On synthetic scenes, the proposed method achieves 28-31x runtime speedup compared to NeRF.
On synthetic scenes, the proposed method delivers 1.4-2.8 dB average PSNR improvement over NeRF without any customized parallelism requirement.

claim_records.text: The proposed Low-Light NeRF (LLNeRF) approach enhances scene representation and synthesizes normal-light novel views directly from sRGB low-light images in an unsupervised manner.
The core of LLNeRF is a decomposition of radiance field learning that enables joint enhancement of illumination, noise reduction, and color distortion correction with NeRF optimization.
LLNeRF produces novel view images with proper lighting and vivid colors and details given a collection of camera-finished low dynamic range (8-bits/channel) images from a low-light scene.
Experiments demonstrate that LLNeRF outperforms existing low-light enhancement methods and NeRF methods.

claim_records.text: NeRF requires querying a deep Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) millions of times, leading to slow rendering times even on modern GPUs.
Real-time rendering is possible by utilizing thousands of tiny MLPs instead of one single large MLP.

Combining the divide-and-conquer tiny MLP strategy with further optimizations accelerates rendering by three orders of magnitude compared to the original NeRF model without incurring high storage costs.

claim_records.text: Existing Human NeRF methods for reconstructing 3D humans typically rely on multiple 2D images from multi-view cameras or monocular videos captured from fixed camera views.
SHERF is the first generalizable Human NeRF model for recovering animatable 3D humans from a single input image.
SHERF extracts and encodes 3D human representations in canonical space, enabling rendering and animation from free views and poses.
SHERF uses a bank of 3D-aware hierarchical features including global, point-level, and pixel-aligned features to facilitate informative encoding.
SHERF uses a feature fusion transformer to effectively integrate the 3D-aware hierarchical feature bank.

Extensive experiments on THuman, RenderPeople, ZJU_MoCap, and HuMMan datasets demonstrate that SHERF achieves state-of-the-art performance, with better generalizability for novel view and pose synthesis.

claim_records.text: The Explicit-NeRF-QA dataset uses 22 3D objects with diverse geometries, textures, and material complexities to train four typical explicit NeRF models across five parameter levels.
A large scale subjective experiment in lab environment collected subjective scores from 21 viewers for rendered NeRF samples to processed video sequences (PVS).

claim_records.text: A major reason existing diffusion-prior NeRF editing work fails to produce reasonable geometry in uncovered regions is the high diversity of synthetic contents from the diffusion model, which hinders the radiance field from converging to a crisp and deterministic geometry.

claim_records.text: Standard NeRF uses straight rays and fails to handle complicated light path changes caused by refraction and reflection, preventing successful synthesis of transparent or specular objects.
NeRRF takes object silhouette as input and uses marching tetrahedra with progressive encoding to reconstruct the geometry of non-Lambertian objects.
NeRRF models refraction and reflection effects of the object in a unified framework using Fresnel terms.
NeRRF proposes a virtual cone supersampling technique to achieve efficient and effective anti-aliasing.
NeRRF is benchmarked on different shapes, backgrounds and Fresnel terms on both real-world and synthetic datasets.
NeRRF qualitatively and quantitatively benchmarks rendering results of editing applications including material editing, object replacement/insertion, and environment illumination estimation.

3DGS-DET achieves an improvement of +6.0 on mAP@0.25 over NeRF-Det++ on the ScanNet dataset.
3DGS-DET achieves an improvement of +7.8 on mAP@0.5 over NeRF-Det++ on the ScanNet dataset.

NeRF extensions such as NeRD can perform decomposition but struggle to accurately recover detailed illumination, significantly limiting realism.
The proposed reflectance decomposition network can estimate shape, BRDF, and per-image illumination given a set of object images captured under varying illumination.
Neural-PIL is an illumination integration network that replaces a costly illumination integral operation in the rendering with a simple network query.
Novel smooth manifold auto-encoders are used to learn deep low-dimensional priors on BRDF and illumination representations.
The proposed decompositions result in considerably better BRDF and light estimates, enabling more accurate novel view-synthesis and relighting compared to prior art.
