claim_records.text: NeRF generates a volumetric representation called a radiance field that is capable of creating color and density for every point within the relevant 3D space, rather than directly restoring the whole 3D scene geometry.
NeRF uses an interpolation approach to produce new 3D reconstructed views of complicated scenes from 2D images.

CAMPARI simultaneously learns a camera generator and an image generator, enabling use of complex camera distributions without manual tuning, and represents scenes through foreground and background decomposition for 3D-consistent representations and accurate camera distribution recovery.
CAMPARI surpasses baseline models that heavily depend on accurately matched camera distributions, due to its performance without camera parameter tuning.
CAMPARI faces the challenge of generating inward-facing faces compared to the traditional hollow face illusion where convex faces appear concave.
Pix2NeRF introduces a pipeline to generate NeRF from a single input image, built upon π-GAN which maps latent codes to radiance fields.
Pix2NeRF employs an unsupervised approach and can be trained with independent images, with potential applications in 3D avatar generation, novel view synthesis, and super-resolution.
A limitation of Pix2NeRF is its current restriction to work with only one category per dataset, impeding its ability to generalize to new categories.
Pix2NeRF is built on top of π-GAN but is not limited to using π-GAN as its backbone; newer generative NeRF models such as EG3D may achieve better visual quality if used as a backbone.

NeRF uses a deep neural network to represent complex scenes in a fully connected, non-convolutional way, with input as a continuous 5D coordinate and output as volume density and view-dependent emitted radiance at that spatial location.
The 5D coordinate space in NeRF includes three dimensions for spatial coordinates (x,y,z) and two dimensions for camera viewing angles (θ,φ).
NeRF uses classic volume rendering techniques to synthesize views and is optimized using a set of images with known camera poses.
NeRF introduces positional encoding and a hierarchical sampling strategy to address the inefficiency of the basic implementation.
Using input viewing direction, NeRF can represent non-Lambertian effects such as specularities.
NeRF uses a separate neural continuous volume representation network for each scene.

claim_records.text: The introduced single-view volumetric field reconstruction technique models unknown volumetric field distributions using an unconditional diffusion model trained on a benchmark dataset of 1,000 synthetically simulated volumetric density fields.

fact_fields.method: unconditional diffusion model for single-view volumetric field reconstruction

claim_records.text: The neural diffusion model for volumetric field reconstruction is trained on the latent codes of a novel, diffusion-friendly monoplanar representation.
A physically-based differentiable volume renderer is employed to provide gradients with respect to light transport in the latent space for the volumetric reconstruction pipeline.

The reconstruction of internal density distribution of highly dense volumes is widely considered nearly impossible due to high uncertainty in the light scattering process and presence of vanishing gradients, and this limitation can only be alleviated by incorporating prior information during reconstruction.

The proposed approach employs a diffusion prior to guide a Physically-based Differentiable Volume Renderer (PDVR) toward reconstructing a plausible volumetric field, by considering the gradient of the image loss with respect to the learned latent space representation to control variations in the diffusion step.

fact_fields.method: diffusion prior guided Physically-based Differentiable Volume Renderer (PDVR)

claim_records.text: The diffusion model for volumetric reconstruction is trained on a dataset of 1,000 synthetically simulated cumulus cloud volumetric density fields, using a novel diffusion-friendly representation for decoding.

The renderer is coupled with the diffusion model to reconstruct radiance parameters using the prior for the density distribution but not for its appearance, so the 3D density field can be trained solely on the prior without requiring images of all possible backgrounds and light scattering effects.
The work contributes a large database of 3D cumulus cloud-like density fields generated using numerical fluid simulation.
The work contributes a 3D cloud decoder utilizing a novel diffusion-friendly monoplanar representation, trained jointly on a subset of the cumulus cloud density field database.

The work proposes a novel Parametric Diffusion Posterior Sampling (PDPS) technique utilizing a shape-centric prior with a physically-based differentiable volume renderer, and is the first approach that integrates an unconditional diffusion model trained on volumetric density distributions with a differentiable volume renderer.
The proposed approach demonstrates potential across tasks including single- and multi-view reconstruction, and volume super-resolution.

claim_records.text: Hyb-NeRF is a neural radiance field with multi-resolution hybrid encoding that represents scenes using different encoding strategies from coarse-to-fine resolution levels: memory-efficient learnable positional features at coarse resolutions, and fast-optimizing hash-based feature grids with local details at fine resolutions.
Cone tracing-based features are embedded in the learnable positional encoding of Hyb-NeRF to eliminate encoding ambiguity and reduce aliasing artifacts.

fact_fields.method: cone tracing-based feature embedding in learnable positional encoding

claim_records.text: Extensive experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets show Hyb-NeRF achieves faster rendering speed, better rendering quality, and lower memory footprint compared to previous state-of-the-art methods.
On the ficus scene in Blender, Hyb-NeRF with 16.4M parameters achieves 35.85 PSNR and 0.986 SSIM, while JNGP with 24.4M parameters achieves 33.23 PSNR and 0.981 SSIM.

fact_fields.method: quantitative comparison on Blender ficus scene

claim_records.text: Hyb-NeRF's multi-resolution hybrid encoding concatenates coarse-level learnable positional features and fine-level hash-based dense grids of trainable features to represent input position x, resulting in a significantly lower memory footprint and higher quality representation of synthetic and real-world scenes.
All Hyb-NeRF models can reconstruct high-quality radiance fields in 9 minutes.

Hyb-NeRF's smallest model with 8.4M trainable parameters takes 4 minutes to achieve better rendering quality than state-of-the-art methods while requiring substantially less memory than previous and concurrent voxel-based methods.

EvaSurf learns an implicit texture embedded with a set of Gaussian lobes to capture view-dependent information for high-fidelity rendering.

EvaSurf can reconstruct high-quality appearance and accurate mesh on both synthetic and real-world datasets.
EvaSurf can be trained in 1-2 hours using a single GPU.
EvaSurf can run on mobile devices at over 40 FPS.
The final package required for EvaSurf rendering takes up only 40-50 MB.

Mip-VoG is an explicit multiscale representation with a deferred architecture designed for real-time anti-aliasing rendering.
Mip-VoG uses a density Mip-VoG for scene geometry and a feature Mip-VoG paired with a small MLP for view-dependent color.
Mip-VoG encodes scene scale using the level of detail (LOD) derived from ray differentials.
Mip-VoG uses quadrilinear interpolation to map a queried 3D location to its features and density from two neighboring downsampled voxel grids.
Mip-VoG is the first approach to offer multiscale training and real-time anti-aliasing rendering simultaneously.
Experiments on multiscale datasets show that Mip-VoG outperforms state-of-the-art real-time rendering baselines.

claim_records.text: NeILF++ is a differentiable rendering framework that performs joint geometry, material, and lighting estimation from multi-view images.

NeILF++ formulates static scene lighting as one neural incident light field (NeILF) and one outgoing neural radiance field (NeRF), departing from prior methods that assume a simplified environment map or co-located flashlights.

NeILF++ unites incident and outgoing light fields through physically-based rendering and surface inter-reflections to disentangle scene geometry, material, and lighting from image observations in a physically-based manner.

NeILF++ achieves state-of-the-art results in geometry reconstruction quality, material estimation accuracy, and novel view rendering fidelity across several datasets.
NeILF++ is presented as a novel differentiable rendering framework for joint geometry, material, and lighting estimation from multi-view images.

claim_records.text: CLIP-NeRF is a multi-modal 3D object manipulation method for neural radiance fields.

CLIP-NeRF leverages the joint language-image embedding space of the Contrastive Language-Image Pre-Training (CLIP) model to enable NeRF manipulation using either a short text prompt or an exemplar image.

fact_fields.method: CLIP-NeRF leveraging CLIP joint language-image embedding space

claim_records.text: CLIP-NeRF uses a disentangled conditional NeRF architecture that allows individual control over both shape and appearance.
In CLIP-NeRF, shape conditioning is achieved by applying a learned deformation field to positional encoding, while color conditioning is deferred to the volumetric rendering stage.

fact_fields.method: CLIP-NeRF shape and color conditioning design

claim_records.text: CLIP-NeRF designs two code mappers that take a CLIP embedding as input and update latent codes to reflect the targeted editing, bridging the disentangled latent representation to the CLIP embedding.
The CLIP-NeRF code mappers are trained with a CLIP-based matching loss to ensure manipulation accuracy.

fact_fields.method: CLIP-NeRF code mapper training with CLIP-based matching loss

claim_records.text: CLIP-NeRF proposes an inverse optimization method that accurately projects an input image to latent codes for manipulation, enabling editing on real images.
CLIP-NeRF is evaluated via extensive experiments on a variety of text prompts and exemplar images, and provides an intuitive interface for interactive editing.
The CLIP-NeRF implementation is available at https://cassiepython.github.io/clipnerf/.

claim_records.text: NeRF and its variants require a lengthy training time ranging from hours to days for a single scene.
The presented voxel grid optimization approach achieves NeRF-comparable quality and converges rapidly from scratch in less than 15 minutes with a single GPU.
The voxel grid optimization representation consists of a density voxel grid for scene geometry and a feature voxel grid with a shallow network for complex view-dependent appearance.
Post-activation interpolation on voxel density is capable of producing sharp surfaces in lower grid resolution.
Direct voxel density optimization is prone to suboptimal geometry solutions, so the optimization process is robustified by imposing several priors.

Evaluation on five inward-facing benchmarks shows that the voxel grid optimization method matches, if not surpasses, NeRF's quality, while taking about 15 minutes to train from scratch for a new scene.

claim_records.text: Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) have low rendering efficiency because rendering a single pixel requires multiple network forwardings.

Existing methods to improve NeRF either reduce the number of required samples or optimize implementation to accelerate network forwarding, but the multiple sampling problem persists due to the intrinsic representation of radiance fields.
Neural Light Fields (NeLF) reduce NeRF computation cost by querying only one single network forwarding per pixel.
Existing NeLF methods require significantly larger network capacities to achieve visual quality close to NeRF, which limits their rendering efficiency in practice.
The proposed Neural Radiance Distribution Field (NeRDF) uses a small network similar to NeRF while preserving rendering speed with a single network forwarding per pixel as in NeLF.
NeRDF models the radiance distribution along each ray with frequency basis, predicts frequency weights using the network, and computes pixel values via volume rendering on radiance distributions.
NeRDF achieves approximately 254x speed-up over NeRF with similar network size, with only a marginal performance decline.

claim_records.text: Implicit neural representation methodologies have inherent computational complexity that constrains attainable frame rates and resolutions in practical applications.
VQ-NeRF reduces the sampling space of NeRF to a lower resolution and reinstates it to the original size using a pre-trained VAE decoder to mitigate the sampling time bottleneck during rendering.
Reconstructing fine texture details of the scene remains challenging with VQ-NeRF's codebook features due to high compression rates.
VQ-NeRF uses a multi-scale NeRF sampling scheme that concurrently optimizes the NeRF model at both compressed and original scales to enhance preservation of fine details.
VQ-NeRF incorporates a semantic loss function to improve geometric fidelity and semantic coherence of 3D reconstructions.
Evaluation on the DTU, BlendMVS, and H3DS datasets confirms VQ-NeRF's superior performance in achieving the optimal trade-off between rendering quality and efficiency.

claim_records.text: Meshes offer high precision for 3D representation, but their dense vertex data complicates editing.
NeRFs deliver excellent rendering quality, but suffer from structural ambiguity that hinders animation and manipulation.

The proposed 3D Hierarchical Proxy Node representation represents an object's shape and texture via a sparse set of hierarchically organized (tree-structured) proxy nodes distributed on its surface and interior.
Each proxy node stores local shape and texture information implicitly encoded by a small MLP within its neighborhood.
Querying any 3D coordinate's properties involves efficient neural interpolation and lightweight decoding from relevant nearby and parent nodes.
The HPR3D framework yields a highly compact representation where nodes align with local semantics, enabling direct drag-and-edit manipulation and offering scalable quality-complexity control.
Extensive experiments across 3D reconstruction and editing demonstrate the HPR3D method's expressive efficiency, high-fidelity rendering quality, and superior editability.

claim_records.text: Neural Radiance Fields typically struggle to reconstruct and render highly specular objects whose appearance varies quickly with changes in viewpoint.
Recent prior NeRF works can render detailed specular appearance of distant environment illumination, but are unable to synthesize consistent reflections of closer content.
Existing improved NeRF specular rendering techniques rely on large computationally-expensive neural networks to model outgoing radiance, which severely limits optimization and rendering speed.

The NeRF-Casting model casts reflection rays from points along each camera ray and traces them through the NeRF representation to render feature vectors which are decoded into color using a small inexpensive network, instead of querying an expensive neural network for outgoing view-dependent radiance at those points.
The NeRF-Casting model outperforms prior methods for view synthesis of scenes containing shiny objects.
NeRF-Casting is the only existing NeRF method that can synthesize photorealistic specular appearance and reflections in real-world scenes.
NeRF-Casting requires comparable optimization time to current state-of-the-art view synthesis models.

claim_records.text: Rendering a single pixel in NeRF requires querying the NeRF network hundreds of times.
Rendering a pixel in Neural Light Field (NeLF) amounts to one single forward pass without ray-marching.
The proposed method uses a deep residual MLP network with 88 layers to effectively learn the light field.
Sufficient data is obtained for training the deep NeLF network by transferring knowledge from a pre-trained NeRF model via data distillation.
On synthetic scenes, the proposed method achieves 26-35x FLOPs reduction per camera ray compared to NeRF.
On synthetic scenes, the proposed method achieves 28-31x runtime speedup compared to NeRF.
On synthetic scenes, the proposed method delivers 1.4-2.8 dB average PSNR improvement over NeRF without any customized parallelism requirement.

claim_records.text: The proposed Low-Light NeRF (LLNeRF) approach enhances scene representation and synthesizes normal-light novel views directly from sRGB low-light images in an unsupervised manner.
The core of LLNeRF is a decomposition of radiance field learning that enables joint enhancement of illumination, noise reduction, and color distortion correction with NeRF optimization.
LLNeRF produces novel view images with proper lighting and vivid colors and details given a collection of camera-finished low dynamic range (8-bits/channel) images from a low-light scene.
Experiments demonstrate that LLNeRF outperforms existing low-light enhancement methods and NeRF methods.

claim_records.text: Existing Human NeRF methods for reconstructing 3D humans typically rely on multiple 2D images from multi-view cameras or monocular videos captured from fixed camera views.
SHERF is the first generalizable Human NeRF model for recovering animatable 3D humans from a single input image.
SHERF extracts and encodes 3D human representations in canonical space, enabling rendering and animation from free views and poses.
SHERF uses a bank of 3D-aware hierarchical features including global, point-level, and pixel-aligned features to facilitate informative encoding.
SHERF uses a feature fusion transformer to effectively integrate the 3D-aware hierarchical feature bank.

Extensive experiments on THuman, RenderPeople, ZJU_MoCap, and HuMMan datasets demonstrate that SHERF achieves state-of-the-art performance, with better generalizability for novel view and pose synthesis.

All tested no-reference metrics on the Explicit-NeRF-QA dataset report very poor results with 0.4 to 0.6 correlations.

claim_records.text: Existing NeRF editing work using diffusion prior struggles to synthesize reasonable geometry in completely uncovered regions.

fact_fields.method: existing NeRF editing work with diffusion prior

claim_records.text: A major reason existing diffusion-prior NeRF editing work fails to produce reasonable geometry in uncovered regions is the high diversity of synthetic contents from the diffusion model, which hinders the radiance field from converging to a crisp and deterministic geometry.
Applying latent diffusion models on real data often yields a textural shift incoherent to the image condition due to auto-encoding errors.
The problems of poor geometry synthesis in uncovered regions and textural shift are further reinforced with the use of pixel-distance losses.
The proposed approach tempers the diffusion model's stochasticity with per-scene customization to address the geometry convergence problem.
The proposed approach mitigates textural shift with masked adversarial training.
During analyses, the commonly used pixel and perceptual losses are found to be harmful in the NeRF inpainting task.

fact_fields.method: analyses of loss functions for NeRF inpainting

claim_records.text: The proposed framework yields state-of-the-art NeRF inpainting results on various real-world scenes.

claim_records.text: RT-NeRF is described as the first algorithm-hardware co-design acceleration of NeRF.
RT-NeRF's algorithm-level rendering pipeline directly computes the geometry of pre-existing points to alleviate inefficiency from commonly adopted uniform point sampling in NeRF.
RT-NeRF leverages a coarse-grained view-dependent computing ordering scheme to eliminate unnecessary processing of invisible points.
RT-NeRF's hardware accelerator adopts a hybrid encoding scheme that adaptively switches between bitmap- or coordinate-based sparsity encoding formats for NeRF's sparse embeddings.

fact_fields.method: RT-NeRF hardware accelerator hybrid encoding scheme

claim_records.text: RT-NeRF's hardware accelerator integrates both a dual-purpose bi-direction adder & search tree and a high-density sparse search unit to coordinate the two encoding formats.
Experiments on eight datasets show RT-NeRF achieves 9.7x to 3,201x throughput improvement while maintaining rendering quality compared with SOTA efficient NeRF solutions.

claim_records.text: Standard NeRF uses straight rays and fails to handle complicated light path changes caused by refraction and reflection, preventing successful synthesis of transparent or specular objects.
NeRRF takes object silhouette as input and uses marching tetrahedra with progressive encoding to reconstruct the geometry of non-Lambertian objects.
NeRRF models refraction and reflection effects of the object in a unified framework using Fresnel terms.
NeRRF proposes a virtual cone supersampling technique to achieve efficient and effective anti-aliasing.
NeRRF is benchmarked on different shapes, backgrounds and Fresnel terms on both real-world and synthetic datasets.
NeRRF qualitatively and quantitatively benchmarks rendering results of editing applications including material editing, object replacement/insertion, and environment illumination estimation.

Directly processing NeRF weights leads to better performance on NeRF-Language tasks compared to approaches that rely on either 2D or 3D representations derived from NeRFs.

claim_records.text: LLaNA is the first general-purpose NeRF-language assistant capable of performing new tasks such as NeRF captioning and Q&A.
LLaNA's method directly processes the weights of the NeRF's MLP to extract information about the represented objects without the need to render images or materialize 3D data structures.
A dataset of NeRFs with text annotations for various NeRF-language tasks was built with no human intervention.
A benchmark was developed based on the NeRF text annotation dataset to evaluate the NeRF understanding capability of LLaNA's method.
Processing NeRF weights performs favourably against extracting 2D or 3D representations from NeRFs, as shown by benchmark results.

claim_records.text: 3DGS-DET introduces 3D Gaussian Splatting into indoor 3D Object Detection for the first time.
3DGS-DET incorporates 2D Boundary Guidance to significantly enhance the spatial distribution of Gaussian blobs, resulting in clearer differentiation between objects and their background.

3DGS-DET proposes a Box-Focused Sampling strategy using 2D boxes to generate object probability distribution in 3D space, allowing effective probabilistic sampling in 3D to retain more object blobs and reduce noisy background blobs.
3DGS-DET achieves an improvement of +6.0 on mAP@0.25 over NeRF-Det++ on the ScanNet dataset.
3DGS-DET achieves an improvement of +7.8 on mAP@0.5 over NeRF-Det++ on the ScanNet dataset.
3DGS-DET achieves an improvement of +14.9 on mAP@0.25 over NeRF-Det++ on the ARKITScenes dataset.

claim_records.text: VDN-NeRF normalizes view-dependence by distilling invariant information already encoded in learned NeRFs, rather than explicitly modeling underlying factors that cause view-dependent radiance variation.
VDN-NeRF jointly trains NeRFs for view synthesis with view-dependence normalization to attain quality geometry.

fact_fields.method: joint training of NeRF view synthesis with view-dependence normalization

claim_records.text: Experiments show the proposed view-dependence normalization can minimize the effect of shape-radiance ambiguity on geometry, aligning the optimal capacity needed for explaining view-dependent variations.
VDN-NeRF applies to various baselines and significantly improves geometry without changing the volume rendering pipeline, even if the data is captured under a moving light source.

claim_records.text: Neural approaches such as NeRF operate exclusively on radiance (the product of reflectance and illumination) and do not explicitly perform scene decomposition.
NeRF extensions such as NeRD can perform decomposition but struggle to accurately recover detailed illumination, significantly limiting realism.
The proposed reflectance decomposition network can estimate shape, BRDF, and per-image illumination given a set of object images captured under varying illumination.
Neural-PIL is an illumination integration network that replaces a costly illumination integral operation in the rendering with a simple network query.
Novel smooth manifold auto-encoders are used to learn deep low-dimensional priors on BRDF and illumination representations.
The proposed decompositions result in considerably better BRDF and light estimates, enabling more accurate novel view-synthesis and relighting compared to prior art.

claim_records.text: NeRF On-the-go, an uncertainty-based approach, enables robust novel view synthesis in complex in-the-wild scenes using only casually captured image sequences.
NeRF On-the-go efficiently eliminates distractors even when distractors are predominant in captures.
NeRF On-the-go achieves a notably faster convergence speed compared to existing methods.
Comprehensive experiments on various scenes show NeRF On-the-go delivers a significant improvement over state-of-the-art techniques.
Existing NeRF methods manage controlled environments and low occlusion ratios but fall short in render quality especially under high occlusion scenarios.

claim_records.text: NeuDA (Neural Deformable Anchor) is a flexible neural implicit representation leveraging hierarchical voxel grids for high-fidelity implicit surface reconstruction.

fact_fields.method: NeuDA (Neural Deformable Anchor), a neural implicit representation leveraging hierarchical voxel grids

claim_records.text: NeuDA maintains hierarchical anchor grids where each vertex stores a 3D position (anchor) instead of a direct embedding (feature).
NeuDA optimizes anchor grids such that different local geometry structures can be adaptively encoded.
NeuDA introduces a simple hierarchical positional encoding method for the hierarchical anchor structure to flexibly exploit properties of high-frequency and low-frequency geometry and appearance.

fact_fields.method: NeuDA (Neural Deformable Anchor) with hierarchical positional encoding

claim_records.text: Experiments on the DTU and BlendedMVS datasets demonstrate that NeuDA can produce promising mesh surfaces.
Previous works IDR and NeuS overlook spatial context in 3D space when predicting and rendering surfaces, which may fail to capture sharp local topologies such as small holes and structures.

HollowNeRF can achieve a PSNR accuracy gain of up to 1dB using only 56% of the parameters.

claim_records.text: The introduced explicit model for volume data compression based on 3D Gaussian primitives reinterprets collections of 3D Gaussians as an explicit representation of a volume's scalar field and uses a sampling strategy that reconstructs scalar values at spatial locations through weighted aggregation of intersecting Gaussians.

fact_fields.method: explicit 3D Gaussian primitive-based volume data compression model

claim_records.text: The explicit 3D Gaussian volume compression model naturally encodes domain geometry, eliminating the need for mesh storage in unstructured volumes and introducing significantly higher compression opportunities.

fact_fields.method: explicit 3D Gaussian primitive-based volume data compression model

claim_records.text: Compared to existing INRs, the explicit 3D Gaussian volume compression model achieves significant training speed and reconstruction quality improvements on both structured and unstructured volumes, while enabling compression ratios much higher than previous work for unstructured volumes.

fact_fields.method: explicit 3D Gaussian primitive-based volume data compression model

methods: explicit 3D Gaussian primitive-based volume data compression model
claims: The introduced explicit model for volume data compression based on 3D Gaussian primitives reinterprets collections of 3D Gaussians as an explicit representation of a volume's scalar field and uses a sampling strategy that reconstructs scalar values at spatial locations through weighted aggregation of intersecting Gaussians.

claim_records.text: OReX uses a Neural Field as the interpolation prior for 3D shape reconstruction from slices alone, where a modest neural network is trained on input planes to return an inside/outside estimate for a given 3D coordinate.

fact_fields.method: OReX with Neural Field as interpolation prior

claim_records.text: The neural prior in OReX is overly smoothing, which makes capturing high-frequency details the main challenge for this approach.

OReX adopts an iterative estimation architecture and a hierarchical input sampling scheme to encourage coarse-to-fine training, allowing the training process to focus on high frequencies at later stages.

fact_fields.method: Iterative estimation architecture combined with hierarchical input sampling scheme

claim_records.text: A ripple-like effect stemming from the mesh extraction step is identified and analyzed in OReX, and it is mitigated by regularizing the spatial gradients of the indicator function around input in/out boundaries during network training.

fact_fields.method: Regularization of spatial gradients of the indicator function around input in/out boundaries during network training

claim_records.text: OReX demonstrates robustness, accuracy, and good scalability with input size, and reports state-of-the-art results compared to previous approaches and recent potential solutions through extensive qualitative and quantitative experimentation.

claims: OReX uses a Neural Field as the interpolation prior for 3D shape reconstruction from slices alone, where a modest neural network is trained on input planes to return an inside/outside estimate for a given 3D coordinate.
The neural prior in OReX is overly smoothing, which makes capturing high-frequency details the main challenge for this approach.

OReX adopts an iterative estimation architecture and a hierarchical input sampling scheme to encourage coarse-to-fine training, allowing the training process to focus on high frequencies at later stages.

A ripple-like effect stemming from the mesh extraction step is identified and analyzed in OReX, and it is mitigated by regularizing the spatial gradients of the indicator function around input in/out boundaries during network training.

OReX demonstrates robustness, accuracy, and good scalability with input size, and reports state-of-the-art results compared to previous approaches and recent potential solutions through extensive qualitative and quantitative experimentation.

assertions.source_quote: Foundational NeRF addresses novel-view synthesis by optimizing a scene-specific MLP from posed RGB images. The network represents a continuous 5D radiance field FΘ(x,d)→(c,σ): density σ is predicted from 3D position alone, while RGB color c can depend on position and viewing direction. The original architecture processes position through eight 256-channel ReLU layers, emits density and a 256-dimensional feature, then combines that feature with direction through a 128-channel ReLU layer to produce view-dependent color. assertions.source_quote: The rendering operator is the bridge between the continuous field and supervised 2D images. For each pixel, NeRF casts a camera ray, evaluates 5D coordinates at sampled points along it, composites the resulting colors and densities with differentiable volume rendering, and compares the rendered pixel color with the observed image. Because this compositing procedure is differentiable, gradients from the image reconstruction loss update the MLP weights using only training images and their known camera poses. The original method also uses positional encoding to expose high-frequency coordinate variation and hierarchical coarse-to-fine sampling to concentrate evaluations where they are expected to affect the rendered ray; these are components of the foundational training strategy, distinct from later systems that replace or cache the MLP for speed. assertions.source_quote: The first classification criterion is what a method stores or queries. The foundational NeRF is a continuous, scene-specific neural field represented by an MLP: a 3D position and viewing direction are network inputs, while density and emitted color are outputs. This differs from explicitly cached or decomposed scene structures such as sparse tensors, low-rank tensors, hash tables, and their combinations, which later work uses to change training, rendering, memory, or editing trade-offs rather than to define the original 5D radiance-field formulation. assertions.source_quote: A third criterion is how samples become pixels. assertions.source_quote: Efficiency-oriented methods should be distinguished from the foundational formulation rather than merged into it. Baking into sparse voxel grids, polygon textures, hash or hybrid feature encodings, vector-quantized sampling, or real-time rasterization pipelines changes where features are stored, how rays or fragments are processed, and which hardware path is used. These approaches may target faster optimization, interactive rendering, lower memory, or mobile deployment, but they do not alter the definition of the original continuous MLP-based NeRF or its differentiable volume-rendering objective. assertions.source_quote: At the representation level, the original paper defines a 5D vector-valued function whose conceptual input is a 3D location x=(x,y,z) and a 2D viewing direction (θ,φ), and whose output is color c=(r,g,b) and density σ. In the implemented network, direction is represented by a 3D Cartesian unit vector d. The learned mapping is written as FΘ:(x,d)→(c,σ), where Θ denotes the MLP parameters. This coordinate-based definition means the field can in principle be queried at continuous positions rather than only at fixed grid cells, although every rendered image uses a finite set of sampled queries. assertions.source_quote: The output dependence is deliberately asymmetric. Density σ is predicted from position x alone, making it a view-invariant scalar field that controls how strongly a spatial location absorbs or occludes light. RGB color c is allowed to depend on both x and the ray direction d, so the same occupied location can have different emitted radiance when seen from different viewpoints. This design gives NeRF a single occupancy-like field for compositing while retaining enough directional freedom to represent non-Lambertian appearance, including view-dependent highlights. It does not, however, explicitly recover separate physical material, lighting, roughness, or normal fields. assertions.source_quote: The original MLP architecture enforces that asymmetry in two stages. Eight fully connected ReLU layers, each with 256 channels, first process only the 3D position x. Their output produces the scalar density σ and a 256-dimensional intermediate feature vector. That feature vector is concatenated with the camera ray's viewing direction d and passed through one additional fully connected ReLU layer with 128 channels, which outputs the view-dependent RGB color. Consequently, position determines both occupancy and a local appearance descriptor, while the final color can be modulated by view direction. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:3_neural_radiance_field_scene_representation:0:e6a7774107f3:claim:2f4a62451a0d]

assertions.source_quote: A camera ray supplies the path along which the field is evaluated. For a pixel, NeRF writes the ray as r(t)=o+td, where o is the ray origin, d is the unit viewing direction, and t indexes distance along the ray. Nearby points along this ray correspond to different spatial locations that the network may report as empty, transparent, or occupied. The renderer does not look for a single surface intersection; instead it integrates color and density through the volume traversed by the ray. This volumetric view is what lets the model represent soft or layered occupancy during optimization even when the final scene appears solid. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:abstract:claim:c90f7f8b0c04] [E:arxiv:2408.03356:section:abstract:4:1447cd6be2ee:claim:6dac674e7eed]

assertions.source_quote: The continuous rendering model assigns color to a ray by integrating emitted color weighted by density and accumulated transmittance. With σ(r(t)) as density, c(r(t),d) as directional color, and T(t) as the probability that light travels without occlusion from the near bound to t, the integral is C(r)=∫ c(r(t),d) σ(r(t)) T(t) dt, with T(t)=exp(−∫_0^t σ(r(s))ds). Higher density at a point increases that point's contribution, while earlier density reduces the contribution of points farther along the ray through exponential attenuation. [E:arxiv:2408.03356:section:abstract:4:1447cd6be2ee:claim:6dac674e7eed]

assertions.source_quote: The differentiability of this compositing rule is the key to learning NeRF from images alone, given camera poses. Sampled coordinates and directions are fed to the MLP, its colors and densities are substituted into the ray-color sum, and the resulting pixel colors are compared with ground-truth observed pixels. Gradients of the image reconstruction loss propagate through the compositing weights and color terms back to the network parameters. The original method therefore does not require 3D ground-truth density or surface labels; the photometric discrepancy between rendered and observed views supplies the training signal. assertions.source_quote: Uniform quadrature can be wasteful because many samples fall in free space or behind opaque content. The original NeRF therefore trains a coarse network and a fine network rather than relying on one uniform sample set. The coarse pass uses N_c stratified samples along the ray, evaluates them with the same volume-rendering equation, and forms sample weights w_i=T_i(1−exp(−σ_iδ_i)). After normalizing these weights, NeRF treats them as a piecewise-constant probability distribution over ray distance and uses inverse transform sampling to draw N_f additional samples in regions expected to affect the image. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:5_2_hierarchical_volume_sampling:0:7c4cd481bcd3:claim:c7a0415d23ab]

assertions.source_quote: The method's contribution is therefore best understood as an end-to-end learned volume-rendering pipeline, not merely as an MLP that predicts colors. A sparse set of calibrated 2D images defines the supervision; the MLP defines a continuous field of density and directional emitted color; ray marching and quadrature define how to form pixels; and differentiable alpha compositing defines how photometric errors update the field. The original method also introduces positional encoding and hierarchical sampling, with hierarchical sampling allocating more network evaluations to parts of each ray that are likely to matter. assertions.source_quote: The applicability boundary of the foundational model is narrower than its later family of extensions. It is a scene-specific representation: a separate continuous MLP is optimized for each scene from posed images, rather than a single network that directly reconstructs arbitrary unseen scenes. Its native output is density and view-dependent emitted radiance for novel-view rendering. The original formulation does not itself provide interactive rendering, an explicit level-set surface, editable semantic parts, a full bidirectional light-transport simulation, or a real-time mobile graphics pipeline; those goals motivate later architectures and extensions. assertions.source_quote: The computational cost follows directly from the rendering mechanism. Every pixel requires a ray, every ray requires many point samples, and every sample requires an MLP evaluation. The original hierarchical strategy improves sample allocation but still evaluates a large neural network at many positions for each image. Later acceleration methods may bake features into sparse voxels, use polygon rasterization, introduce hash or hybrid encodings, or otherwise cache and restructure the field. Those systems can inherit NeRF's image-synthesis goal, but they are implementation or representation changes around the foundational continuous-field and volume-compositing formulation rather than prerequisites for defining it. assertions.source_quote: The central experimental setup of foundational NeRF is per-scene optimization from a sparse set of 2D images with known camera poses. The independent object being fit is the MLP-defined field FΘ:(x,d)→(c,σ), while the measured outcome is whether images rendered from held-out camera views match real observations. There is no separate 3D density label or surface annotation in this basic setup: sampled coordinates and directions are passed through the network, volume rendering produces pixel colors, and the residual between synthesized and ground-truth images supplies gradients to Θ. assertions.source_quote: Along the representation dimension, the tested hypothesis is that a continuous coordinate-based MLP can encode both occupancy-like geometry and view-dependent appearance in one scene-specific function. The architecture separates these roles by predicting σ from x alone and c from x together with d. In the original network, eight fully connected ReLU layers with 256 channels process position and output density plus a 256-dimensional feature; concatenating that feature with the viewing direction and applying one 128-channel ReLU layer yields RGB. This supports the method's intended comparison against prior neural rendering and view-synthesis approaches: geometry need not be stored as a fixed mesh or voxel grid, and non-Lambertian color can vary with viewpoint while density remains tied to spatial location. assertions.source_quote: The sampling experiment compares dense or uniform evaluation with coarse-to-fine allocation. Uniformly evaluating the network at many points is inefficient because free space and occluded regions can receive repeated queries even though they contribute little to the image. assertions.source_quote: Later systems provide useful contrast points, but their reported speed, memory, or quality numbers are not directly comparable to the original NeRF experiment unless the representation, samples, hardware, datasets, and training schedule are matched. Sparse voxel baking and polygon rasterization replace repeated MLP ray queries with cached features or standard graphics pipelines; hash, tensor, and hybrid encodings alter where scene features are stored; and multiscale or reflection methods add different representations and rendering assumptions. These comparisons identify computational and modeling trade-offs, but they do not test the same exact baseline as the original continuous-MLP and differentiable-volume-rendering formulation. assertions.source_quote: Accordingly, the appropriate conclusion from this experiment-focused explanation is not a cross-family benchmark ranking. assertions.source_quote: The main open limitation of foundational NeRF is computational rather than merely implementational. Rendering a pixel requires marching a camera ray through the scene, evaluating a large MLP at hundreds of sampled positions, and integrating density and radiance from those queries; the original hierarchical sampler reduces wasted samples but does not remove this many-query-per-pixel structure. As a result, the basic formulation is poorly matched to interactive visualization, especially when high resolution or many views must be rendered. Later acceleration systems address this by baking sparse voxel features, using polygon rasterization, or replacing plain MLP storage with hash grids, tensors, or hybrid encodings, which shows that speed is a separate design objective from defining the continuous radiance field. Rendering a pixel requires marching a camera ray through the scene, evaluating a large MLP at hundreds of sampled positions, and integrating density and radiance from those queries; the original hierarchical sampler reduces wasted samples but does not remove this many-query-per-pixel structure. As a result, the basic formulation is poorly matched to interactive visualization, especially when high resolution or many views must be rendered. Later acceleration systems address this by baking sparse voxel features, using polygon rasterization, or replacing plain MLP storage with hash grids, tensors, or hybrid encodings, which shows that speed is a separate design objective from defining the continuous radiance field. assertions.source_quote: The acceleration trade-off is not free. Caching a NeRF into explicit data structures can improve rendering speed, but it increases memory use; for example, SNeRG's sparse volumetric textures are described as requiring substantial GPU memory, which prevents deployment on common mobile devices. MobileNeRF instead moves the deferred view-dependent decode into a small shader-stage MLP behind textured polygons so standard z-buffer rasterization can exploit commodity GPU parallelism. These systems demonstrate that the foundational MLP's compact functional description and later real-time data structures optimize different points in the compute, memory, and hardware-compatibility space. assertions.source_quote: A second open problem is geometric ambiguity. The photometric renderer only needs a volume whose alpha-composited colors explain the observed images; it does not require a unique zero-thickness surface. NeRF can therefore rely on dense regions of the volume, transparency, or layering to approximate complex appearance and geometry, and a high-quality rendered view does not uniquely determine a mesh. NeRF++ explicitly identifies a shape-radiance ambiguity in radiance fields, while later mesh-extraction work notes that radiance fields optimized for novel view synthesis are commonly not explicit level-set surfaces and may rely on transparency or layering. Consequently, density σ should not automatically be interpreted as a signed-distance field or as a guaranteed surface reconstruction. assertions.source_quote: View-dependent color intensifies this geometry problem under non-Lambertian or changing-light conditions. Allowing color to depend on viewing direction is essential for representing specular and other directional appearance in the original model, but it also gives the network capacity to explain image variation through radiance rather than invariant geometry. VDN-NeRF states that shape-radiance ambiguity remains inevitable and proposes view-dependence normalization to reduce its effect on geometry without changing the volume-rendering pipeline. This supports a bounded conclusion: the foundational representation is directly suited to image synthesis, but accurate geometry extraction may require additional constraints, normalization, or extraction methods. assertions.source_quote: Specular reflections reveal another modeling boundary. Directional emitted color lets a point change appearance with the outgoing viewing direction, but the original field does not trace incoming reflection paths or separate nearby reflected content from the material response. Later ray-traced NeRF work reports that prior methods can improve detailed specular appearance from distant environment illumination but cannot consistently synthesize reflections of closer content, and that expensive neural outgoing-radiance networks also limit optimization and rendering speed. Thus, view-dependent RGB in foundational NeRF is a phenomenological radiance output, not a complete bidirectional reflection or global-illumination simulation. assertions.source_quote: The original representation is scene-specific and optimization-based. A separate neural continuous volume is fitted to each scene from posed images, and the training signal depends on known camera poses and a photometric rendering loss. assertions.source_quote: Representation choice also affects downstream controllability. Plain MLPs, sparse tensors, low-rank tensors, hash tables, and composite structures have different trade-offs; PVD specifically notes that hash-table-based representations train and render quickly but lack clear geometric meaning, which hampers spatial-relation-aware editing. This means that replacing the foundational MLP solely for speed can make manipulation or semantic interpretation harder, while converting representations after training may be needed to match a downstream task. The limitation is therefore not a simple ranking among backbones: rendering speed, training speed, memory, geometric interpretability, and editability can conflict. assertions.source_quote: Integration with conventional graphics pipelines is another unresolved issue for the native model. Foundational NeRF relies on specialized volumetric ray marching rather than the meshes and z-buffered rasterization used by most standard graphics pipelines. Later polygon-based and Unreal Engine integrations explicitly introduce textured polygons, optimized geometry, levels of detail, or engine rasterization to obtain interactive and 4K rendering workflows. These systems indicate that the original continuous volume is not directly equivalent to an asset format for standard engines, physics simulation, or hardware-accelerated polygon pipelines. unsupported_claims.source_quote: The rendering operator is the bridge between the continuous field and supervised 2D images. For each pixel, NeRF casts a camera ray, evaluates 5D coordinates at sampled points along it, composites the resulting colors and densities with differentiable volume rendering, and compares the rendered pixel color with the observed image. Because this compositing procedure is differentiable, gradients from the image reconstruction loss update the MLP weights using only training images and their known camera poses. The original method also uses positional encoding to expose high-frequency coordinate variation and hierarchical coarse-to-fine sampling to concentrate evaluations where they are expected to affect the rendered ray; these are components of the foundational training strategy, distinct from later systems that replace or cache the MLP for speed. unsupported_claims.source_quote: The applicability boundary of the foundational model is narrower than its later family of extensions. It is a scene-specific representation: a separate continuous MLP is optimized for each scene from posed images, rather than a single network that directly reconstructs arbitrary unseen scenes. Its native output is density and view-dependent emitted radiance for novel-view rendering. The original formulation does not itself provide interactive rendering, an explicit level-set surface, editable semantic parts, a full bidirectional light-transport simulation, or a real-time mobile graphics pipeline; those goals motivate later architectures and extensions. unsupported_claims.source_quote: Along the representation dimension, the tested hypothesis is that a continuous coordinate-based MLP can encode both occupancy-like geometry and view-dependent appearance in one scene-specific function. The architecture separates these roles by predicting σ from x alone and c from x together with d. In the original network, eight fully connected ReLU layers with 256 channels process position and output density plus a 256-dimensional feature; concatenating that feature with the viewing direction and applying one 128-channel ReLU layer yields RGB. This supports the method's intended comparison against prior neural rendering and view-synthesis approaches: geometry need not be stored as a fixed mesh or voxel grid, and non-Lambertian color can vary with viewpoint while density remains tied to spatial location. unsupported_claims.source_quote: The main open limitation of foundational NeRF is computational rather than merely implementational. Rendering a pixel requires marching a camera ray through the scene, evaluating a large MLP at hundreds of sampled positions, and integrating density and radiance from those queries; the original hierarchical sampler reduces wasted samples but does not remove this many-query-per-pixel structure. As a result, the basic formulation is poorly matched to interactive visualization, especially when high resolution or many views must be rendered. Later acceleration systems address this by baking sparse voxel features, using polygon rasterization, or replacing plain MLP storage with hash grids, tensors, or hybrid encodings, which shows that speed is a separate design objective from defining the continuous radiance field.
